input.content:
# Game Concept: The Synaptic Sea

*Created: 2026-10-25*
*Status: Draft*

> **Creative Director Review (CD-PILLARS)**: APPROVED 2026-10-25 (five-pillar revision) — re-check pending on the Pillar 4 intensity upgrade
> **Art Director Review (AD-CONCEPT-VISUAL)**: DIRECTIONS DELIVERED 2026-10-25 — user selected a B-dominant hybrid (see Visual Identity Anchor)
> **Technical Director Review (TD-FEASIBILITY)**: CONCERNS (accepted) 2026-10-25 — HIGH RISK as first written; two scope changes accepted (host-owned save, single-player slice first)
> **Producer Review (PR-SCOPE)**: OPTIMISTIC → adjustments applied 2026-10-25 (VS split, spike phase, widened MVP estimate, 4–6 year horizon)

---

## Elevator Pitch

> It's a co-op survival sim where you keep a ship welded together from dead ships
> alive inside a vast cosmic web, and the deeper you salvage, the less you can
> trust what you see.

Wake in the cryo bay of a derelict. Repair a podcraft. Board the other wrecks
caught in the web, strip their working systems, weld them onto your own hull.
The web notices light and noise. Exposure erodes sanity, and sanity rewrites
what your eyes and instruments tell you.

---

## Core Identity

| Aspect | Detail |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Genre** | Survival sim / cosmic horror, with functional (not freeform) base-building |
| **Platform** | PC (Steam / Epic), Windows first |
| **Target Audience** | Systems-literate explorers who want co-op dread (see Player Profile) |
| **Player Count** | 1–4. Single-player first; online co-op gated behind the proven slice |
| **Session Length** | 60–120 minutes |
| **Monetization** | Premium, Early Access (provisional — not yet decided) |
| **Estimated Scope** | Large (48–72 months, solo) |
| **Comparable Titles** | Project Zomboid, Barotrauma, Oxygen Not Included |

---

## Core Fantasy

"The ship is alive because we keep it alive, minute by minute — and we're the
only ones awake, and we're starting to understand what that means."

Cooperative self-sufficiency under cosmic dread. The player's base is not a
house they found; it is a body they assembled from the corpses of other ships,
and every loop in it is something they personally keep breathing. The horror
is not that the web attacks the ship. It is that the web attacks the crew's
ability to know whether the ship is fine.

The emotional anchor comes directly from the designer's own touchstone: a
Project Zomboid base, built with friends, that becomes self-sufficient and
survivable. This game puts that feeling in a place where "survivable" is never
quite certain and the friends might be hallucinating.

---

## Unique Hook

Like Project Zomboid's long-tail survival loop, **AND ALSO** your base is a
life-support machine welded from other dead ships, and the sanity system is a
perception system: gauges, sprites, salvage and even your crewmates can lie to
you, and the only cure is to check — which costs time, risk or trust.

Why it is not a gimmick:
- It affects gameplay, not aesthetics. A false "fixed" state on a scrubber is
  a death you walked into.
- It is connected to the core fantasy. Co-op matters because crewmates are each
  other's instruments.
- It is novel. Sanity in survival games is usually a stat debuff. Here it is
  misinformation with a verification economy around it.

---

## Player Experience Analysis (MDA Framework)

### Target Aesthetics (What the player FEELS)

| Aesthetic | Priority | How We Deliver It |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Discovery** (exploration, secrets) | 1 | Procedural derelicts with one visible unknown each; web rules learned by observation; lore assembled from fragments; the center as a horizon |
| **Challenge** (obstacle course, mastery) | 2 | Visible life-support graph that fails in traceable ways; Attention management; breach recovery; learning horror tells |
| **Fellowship** (social connection) | 3 | Crew roles (boarder vs. ship-keeper); per-player sanity makes trust a mechanic; a shared home-ship |
| **Fantasy** (make-believe) | 4 | "We are the only ones awake"; a ship that is ours because we welded it |
| **Narrative** (drama, story arc) | 5 | Non-linear lore; the cryo-bay question (who else is in the pods, and why do they keep waking?) |
| **Sensation** (sensory pleasure) | 6 | HD pixel art under a light-as-resource rendering model; flow-coded loops glowing in the dark; adaptive audio (later tier) |
| **Expression** (self-expression) | 7 | Which modules to graft and where — functional, not cosmetic |
| **Submission** (relaxation) | N/A | Deliberately absent |

### Key Dynamics (Emergent player behaviors)

- Players will **go dark** deliberately — running fewer loops, cutting lights —
  to lower the web's attention before a deep sortie.
- Players will **cross-check each other**: "Is that scrubber really green on
  your screen?" becomes normal crew chatter.
- Players will **specialize**: one keeps the ship alive, one boards.
- Players will **weigh a module's value against the noise of taking it**.
- Players will **develop house rules for low-sanity crewmates** (disarm them,
  keep them away from the reactor) without the game prescribing it.
- Players will **tell stories about the time the loot was garbage**.

### Core Mechanics (Systems we build)

1. **Life-support graph** — O₂, heat and power as a continuously simulated,
   visible graph across welded sections; failures propagate along edges and
   render as physical trails (frost, mist, scorch, drip).
2. **Modular welding** — derelict sections are grafted onto the home-ship,
   joining their nodes to the graph and their collision to one composite body;
   sections can be cut away.
3. **Attention** — the web accumulates attention from light, noise, power use
   and depth (depth sets the baseline); shown in the world, never as a hidden
   meter; crossing thresholds flips boarding into breach.
4. **Sanity and hallucination** — per-player sanity degrades with exposure;
   low sanity drives a client-side presentation filter that corrupts perception
   (entities, system states, crewmates, salvage) while the simulation stays
   authoritative and at least one channel of truth remains.
5. **Procedural derelicts** — hand-authored room kits assembled by a generator
   from a seed, with salvage placed by rules and one externally visible
   unknown per wreck.
6. **Persistence and the failure contract** — host-owned, versioned saves of
   the composite ship, world seed plus deltas, and per-player progression;
   losing the ship or a body never loses knowledge.

---

## Player Motivation Profile

### Primary Psychological Needs Served

| Need | How This Game Satisfies It | Strength |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Autonomy** | Which derelict, which module, how deep, how loud, who boards and who stays | Core |
| **Competence** | Reading a failing loop, surviving a breach, learning what each horror does before it does it, learning when to doubt your eyes | Core |
| **Relatedness** | Crew roles; crewmates as each other's instruments; a shared ship; the cryo-bay mystery | Core (co-op), Supporting (solo via the ship-as-body) |

### Player Type Appeal (Bartle Taxonomy)

- [x] **Explorers** — Primary. Understanding the web's rules, the derelicts' stories, and their own perception.
- [x] **Socializers** — Secondary. Crew trust, verification chatter, shared stories of disaster.
- [x] **Achievers** — Light. Ship capability and depth rings as a ladder; no completion checklist.
- [ ] **Killers/Competitors** — Not served. No PvP, no leaderboards; horrors are avoided, not farmed.

### Flow State Design

- **Onboarding curve**: The cryo bay is a single sealed section with one
  failing loop. The first ten minutes teach "see the leak, follow it to the
  source, fix it, watch the gauge agree with the pipe." The first pod hop
  teaches the boarding rhythm; the first Attention threshold teaches breach.
- **Difficulty scaling**: Depth rings raise the Attention baseline, horror
  variety and salvage value together. Outer-ring depletion pushes inward.
- **Feedback clarity**: Every system has a visible moving part and medium.
  Failure is a trail the eye can follow. Attention is heard and seen before it
  acts. Sanity drift starts with instruments disagreeing with the world.
- **Recovery from failure**: Breach is survivable by retreat to the pod. Losing
  the ship or a crewmate loses ship and body, never knowledge: the next crew
  wakes in the cryo bay knowing more. Failure is educational by contract.

---

## Core Loop

### Moment-to-Moment (30 seconds) — two rhythms

- **Boarding rhythm** (deliberate, Zomboid-paced): cut a hatch, listen, sweep a
  light, read a dead ship's gauges, decide whether a module is worth the noise
  of taking it. Every door is a decision.
- **Breach rhythm** (frantic, Barotrauma-paced): the web has noticed. A hull
  section fails, power drops, something wakes. Patch, re-route, retreat.
- **The hinge** is Attention. Light, noise, power spikes and depth raise it; it
  is shown in the world; crossing a line flips the rhythm. Dread is feeling it
  come.

### Short-Term (5–15 minutes) — the sortie

Fly the pod to a derelict → board → find one salvageable system (scrubber,
reactor cell, hull plate, data core) → extract it under rising Attention →
return → weld it in. Every wreck shows one visible unknown from outside; that
is the "one more sortie" pull.

### Session-Level (60–120 minutes)

Pick a target on the web map. Prep (O₂, tools, suppressants). Run 2–4 sorties.
Come home, integrate modules, re-stabilize the graph, read recovered logs.
Natural stop: the ship is stable again. The hook: the log names a deeper wreck.

### Long-Term Progression (days/weeks)

- **Ship capability** — life-support margin, range, hull.
- **Knowledge** — the web's rules, horror tells, decoded lore. Persists across
  crew loss. Some rules shift with depth so the web never becomes solvable.
- **Depth** — rings of the web, each with a higher Attention baseline.
- **Sanity scars** — permanent quirks a character carries.
- There is no win state. The center is a horizon.

### Retention Hooks

- **Curiosity**: the unknown on every wreck; the log that names a deeper one;
  who else is in the cryo pods.
- **Investment**: a ship that is literally assembled from your history.
- **Social**: a crew that needs you to be the sane one tonight.
- **Mastery**: reading the graph faster; knowing a tell; knowing when to doubt.

---

## Game Pillars

### Pillar 1: The World Never Lies
Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only
instruments and perception can be wrong.

*Design test*: a hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe.

### Pillar 2: Dread Before Chaos
Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived
(sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress). This pillar owns tempo and
presentation; Pillar 3 owns causality.

*Design test*: breach fires at a hidden threshold vs. breach preceded by a
10–30 second escalating tell → the tell.

### Pillar 3: The Web Watches
The players' light, noise, power use and restraint raise or lower its
attention. Attention is shown in the world (creaking, flicker, filament
movement), never as a hidden meter. Depth sets the baseline; player action
moves it from there. Restraint and stealth are real strategies.

*Design test*: a flat spawn timer vs. attention-driven escalation → attention.

### Pillar 4: Sanity Rewrites Reality (and Crewmates Are Instruments)
Low sanity changes what the player perceives, not just their stats. Phantom
entities appear (and at depth, real ones hide). Broken things read as fixed and
fixed as broken. Crewmates render as horrors, and friendly harm is possible. A
crate of treasure is garbage once it is home. **No lie is unfalsifiable**: the
truth is always available through the physical world, a second instrument, a
saner crewmate, or time — and checking costs time, risk or trust. At least one
channel of truth always remains. Solo play is supported through the first two
checks; co-op adds the human one.

*Design test*: a hallucination that can never be disproved vs. one that costs
time, risk or trust to disprove → the costly one.
*Secondary test*: −10% move speed vs. a gauge showing a false value → the
false gauge.

### Pillar 5: Deeper Is Richer, Loss Is Not Total
Risk and reward map to depth in the web. The outer ring is kept unsafe by
depletion and wear (scrubbers degrade, salvage runs out), so there is no safe
place to farm forever. **Failure contract**: losing the home-ship or a crewmate
costs ship and body, never knowledge — decoded rules and lore persist, and the
next crew wakes knowing more.

*Design test*: safe farming vs. scarcity that pushes inward → scarcity.

**Intended tension**: Pillar 1 (legible) vs. Pillar 4 (lying). Resolved inside
the game world: the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception
are what can be wrong. The tension is the game.

### Anti-Pillars (What This Game Is NOT)

- **NOT a freeform ship-building sandbox**: welding is functional and modules
  are pre-shaped. Creative construction would dilute Dread Before Chaos and
  Deeper Is Richer.
- **NOT a combat game**: no weapon tree. Tools may repel or distract (flares,
  torches, decoys); nothing levels up from killing — including crewmates.
  Horrors are avoided and survived, not farmed. Protects The Web Watches.
- **NOT intentional PvP**: harm to a crewmate is only ever a sanity failure,
  never a system the game rewards. Protects relatedness.
- **NOT an authored linear story**: no chapters or cutscenes; lore is found and
  assembled. Protects the long tail.
- **NOT a game you win**: no "escape the web" ending in v1.

---

## Visual Identity Anchor

**Direction name**: *What You Light, You Can Read* — a B-dominant hybrid of the
art-director's "The Dark Is the Default" and "Every Pipe Is a Sentence".

**One-line visual rule**: Light is a resource you spend; inside your light,
every pipe is a sentence; outside it, the dark is honest.

**Supporting visual principles**

1. *Darkness is honest; light is a decision.* Rooms are not fogged, they are
   unlit; geometry is there and any source reveals it.
   *Test*: a vignette / fog-of-war mask vs. true 2D occlusion from light
   sources with hard falloff → true occlusion.
2. *Inside the light, state lives in the sprite, not the icon.* Every system
   has a visible moving part and medium; failure renders as a trail (puddle,
   frost, scorch, mist) in the loop's hue.
   *Test*: a status LED vs. a turning rotor with visible fluid → rotor and
   fluid; a "COOLANT LOW" banner vs. a frosted elbow with a drip → the elbow.
3. *Emission is exposure.* Running loops glow in their own hue; with power off
   the ship is lit only by what is running. Every loop you run is a lantern the
   web can see; the web itself is seen only in your own light.
   *Test*: an attention meter vs. more filaments resolving in your light cone
   as attention rises → the filaments.

**Color philosophy**: Near-monochrome cold base (blue-black steel, graphite).
Human light is tungsten amber; alarm is red. Resource loops are flow-coded and
keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O₂ cyan, power amber,
coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey). The web has an oily
iridescence under direct light and otherwise no hue of its own. Deeper rings
do not change hue; they lower ambient and raise the iridescence. **Flesh tones
and violet appear nowhere in the sane world**, so when they appear, it is the
player's sanity, never the location.

**Sanity drift**: instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the
ship), then the light lies (cone reaches further than it does, shadows with no
occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at the pipe edges
and flesh tones enter. **Anchors that never shift**: character sprites, hand
tools, the HUD frame, and the physical radius your light actually reveals when
you walk into it.

**Accessibility coordination** (for `/ux-design`): hue coding must be
redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) for colorblind
players.

**Pipeline note**: this direction puts the main art workload into the 2D
lighting pipeline rather than sprite-state count. The lighting-budget spike is
therefore the first spike, not the last.

---

## Inspiration and References

| Reference | What We Take From It | What We Do Differently | Why It Matters |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| Project Zomboid | Long-tail survival, lived-in detail, "one more day", base-with-friends | The base is mobile, modular, and made of other ships; no neighbourhoods | Validates patience for slow systemic survival and a decade-long EA model |
| Satisfactory | Legible machinery; flows you can read at a glance | The "factory" is a life-support system under eldritch pressure; no scale-up | Validates that watching a machine work is its own reward |
| Stellaris | Slow-reveal galactic horror; a universe that gets worse the more you know | Scale is one ship, not an empire; horror is personal and perceptual | Validates appetite for cosmic dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes |
| Barotrauma | Co-op crew under pressure in a hostile medium; breach rhythm | Boarding rhythm is slow and quiet; sanity is misinformation, not a stat | Validates co-op dread in a 2D vessel |
| Oxygen Not Included | Visible gas/heat/power simulation as the core puzzle | Far smaller graph, in service of dread rather than optimization | Validates a visible life-support graph as a core mechanic |

**Non-game inspirations**: *Beyond the Aquila Rift* (Love, Death & Robots) —
a ship trapped in a web, reality decaying, the kindness of the lie. *Pandorum*
— waking into wrongness aboard a derelict, not knowing how long you slept.

---

## Target Player Profile

| Attribute | Detail |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Age range** | 20–40 |
| **Gaming experience** | Mid-core to hardcore; comfortable with systems and slow pacing |
| **Time availability** | 1–2 hour evening sessions, often scheduled with friends; longer on weekends |
| **Platform preference** | PC, Steam |
| **Current games they play** | Project Zomboid, Barotrauma, Oxygen Not Included, Lethal Company |
| **What they're looking for** | Co-op dread with honest systems; a base that is theirs; a mystery that systems reveal, not cutscenes |
| **What would turn them away** | Jump-scare horror; fast onboarding expectations; freeform creative building; authored endings; PvP |

**Who this is NOT for**: competitors (no PvP or leaderboards), players who
want authored narrative payoff, freeform builders, anyone who needs a fast
start.

---

## Technical Considerations

| Consideration | Assessment |
| ---- | ---- |
| **Recommended Engine** | Godot 4.7.2, GDScript (pinned by `/setup-engine`). TD-FEASIBILITY: nothing argues for another engine; high-level multiplayer fits a small listen-server co-op |
| **Key Technical Challenges** | Composite welded ship (one physics body, sections reparented on weld); life-support graph as pure data separate from the scene tree; server-authoritative design from day one even in single-player; per-client hallucination presentation filter that never touches the simulation; readable procgen from room kits; 2D lighting budget on D3D12 (Windows default since 4.6); versioned saves from v1 |
| **Art Style** | HD pixel art (high-resolution, detailed pixels), 3/4 oblique top-down, light-as-resource rendering |
| **Art Pipeline Complexity** | High — lighting pipeline is the main workload; modular derelict sections are the largest asset sink |
| **Audio Needs** | Adaptive (later tier). Attention and breach tells are audio-first; the ship must breathe |
| **Networking** | Listen-server (host-authoritative) via Godot high-level multiplayer. Host-owned saves, no live host migration. Steam lobby / NAT solution requires a technology evaluation before co-op work. Co-op gated behind the single-player slice |
| **Content Volume** | Full vision: 3 depth rings; several hand-authored room kits; dozens of module types; 4+ horror types; 4 hallucination classes; lore fragment set. Open-ended play; no fixed hours |
| **Procedural Systems** | Derelict interiors from kits + grammar, seeded; salvage placement by rules; host sends seed + deltas |

---

## Risks and Open Questions

### Design Risks
- The two-rhythm loop may not be tense and absorbing for 30+ minutes solo
  (the MVP's single question).
- Intense hallucinations may read as cheap deaths if the cost-to-verify is
  tuned wrong. "No lie is unfalsifiable" must hold in practice, not just on
  paper.
- Crewmates-as-monsters could become griefing-by-proxy without a guard rail
  (pending CD re-check).
- Persistent knowledge could make the web solvable; some rules must shift
  with depth.
- Deep resource simulation could swallow the dread (the Hull Pressure risk).

### Technical Risks (from TD-FEASIBILITY, CONCERNS)
- Authority discipline lapsing during the single-player phase → co-op becomes
  a rewrite. Enforce via ADR and control manifest; periodically run two local
  instances.
- Life-support graph entangled with the scene tree → untestable, unserializable.
- Save format not versioned from v1 → breaks every time a module changes.
- 2D lighting cost unmeasured for 4.7 on D3D12; Forward+ vs. Compatibility
  renderer is reversible and should be decided from spike data.
- Hallucination filter touching simulation state → endless desync bugs. Rule:
  every client receives the true value; corruption is presentation-only, with
  at least one channel of truth remaining, and a true-value debug overlay.
- Steam lobby / NAT traversal is a separate milestone from LAN co-op.
- 4.5–4.7 APIs are past the model's training cutoff; verify against
  `docs/engine-reference/godot/`.

### Market Risks
- Cosmic-horror survival is a niche within a niche; premium EA depends on a
  strong demo and word of mouth.
- Co-op arriving late may disappoint the audience most drawn to the pitch.

### Scope Risks (from PR-SCOPE, OPTIMISTIC → adjusted)
- First game, first engine: 1–3 months of learning folded into the MVP clock.
- HD pixel art throughput likely exceeds code time.
- No velocity data exists; every estimate is low-confidence until the spike
  phase produces some.
- Motivation over a 4–6 year solo horizon, not a deadline, is the real risk.

### Open Questions
- **What do guests keep** from a host-owned world (knowledge? sanity scars?
  nothing?) — for game-designer and creative-director; the save schema waits on
  it.
- **Who is in the other cryo pods, and why do they keep waking?** — for
  narrative-director; it is the failure contract's fiction.
- **Guard rail for crewmates-as-monsters** — pending CD-PILLARS re-check.
- **Renderer choice** (Forward+ vs. Compatibility) — answered by the lighting
  spike.
- **Steam lobby / NAT solution** — technology evaluation before VS-B.

---

## MVP Definition

**Core hypothesis**: The boarding→breach two-rhythm loop, over a visible
life-support graph, is tense and absorbing for a 30+ minute solo session.

**Required for MVP** (single-player):
1. One handmade spawn derelict and one handmade target derelict, with an
   abstracted pod hop between them.
2. Visible O₂ / heat / power graph with propagating, physically rendered
   failures.
3. One weld: attach one section and join its nodes to the graph.
4. Attention with one threshold and one horror behaviour.
5. Sanity as a single hallucination class (false system state), falsifiable by
   the physical world.
6. Save/load v1 with a format version.
7. All state changes through a single command/simulation layer (no networking
   code, no replication).

**Explicitly NOT in MVP**: procedural generation, co-op, multiple horrors,
other hallucination classes, lore, Steam, art at final fidelity, adaptive
audio.

**Kill/continue gate at the end of MVP**: playtest with at least three people
outside the project. If a 30+ minute solo session is not tense and absorbing,
iterate on the loop before any VS-A work. No procgen on an unproven loop.

### Scope Tiers (if budget/time shrinks)

| Tier | Content | Features | Timeline (solo; low confidence until spikes produce velocity) |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| **Spike phase** | Throwaway prototypes | Weld on a moving ship (tilemap + collision + graph merge); graph with spreading failures; save round-trip with version; 2D lighting budget on D3D12 | 4–8 weeks |
| **MVP** | 2 handmade derelicts | Core loop only (list above) + playtest gate | 6–9 months full-time / 10–16 part-time |
| **VS-A** (single-player, **the shippable fallback**) | Outer ring of the web map; one procgen room kit | Procgen derelicts; 2nd horror type; all 4 hallucination classes with falsification checks; one derelict kit at target HD-pixel fidelity under the lighting model | +8–12 months |
| **VS-B** (co-op) | Same content | 2-player LAN listen-server; authority model proven with two local instances | +4–6 months, only after VS-A is complete |
| **Alpha** | 3 depth rings; full kit set; lore fragments | Steam lobbies / NAT; crew scars and knowledge persistence (failure contract); versioned saves; host-owned world + guest carry-over; true-value debug overlay | +12–18 months |
| **Full Vision** | Early Access launch | Polish; adaptive audio; accessibility; onboarding | ~4–6 years total |

**What ships if time runs out**: VS-A, as a small single-player survival-horror
game. Co-op and depth rings are cut; the product is whole.

---

The concept document is written to `design/gdd/game-concept.md` (durable now, under `autonomous`), with the gate outcomes recorded in its status header, the B-dominant Visual Identity Anchor, the upgraded Pillar 4, and the producer's adjusted scope tiers (spike phase → MVP → VS-A solo fallback → VS-B co-op → Alpha → Full Vision, ~4–6 years).

One gate is still open: the creative-director's re-check of the intensified Pillar 4, specifically whether "crewmates as monsters, friendly harm possible" needs a guard rail against griefing-by-proxy. I'll patch the document's header and the open-questions entry when that verdict lands, then give you the final summary and next steps.

The creative-director came back **CONCERNS** again, but on guard rails, not on intensity. The verdict actually calls crewmates-as-monsters "the strongest thing in the revision." The fixes:

1. **P1 names channels no hallucination can touch**: physical consequences (the pipe *looks* fixed but the room still gets cold), the sane palette (every hallucination leaks flesh/violet somewhere, however subtle), and the human channel (voice chat and a crewmate's own light beam are never faked — a monster that speaks in your friend's voice is your friend).
2. **Hidden real monsters still leave footprints** (sound, frost, hull stress). The hallucination hides the body, never the trail.
3. **Friendly harm is system-gated**: only possible while the *attacker's* sanity is verifiably low, so a sane player can't fake it; the victim gets a tell; the game attributes the incident to the web (logs, scars), not to the player.
4. **Phantom salvage gets a field check** (weight, a second scanner, the palette leak) so the trip home is the fallback, not the only way to find out.

I'm applying 1, 2, 4 and the gate/tell/attribution parts of 3 (they protect your intensity rather than dilute it). One point contradicts what you said: the CD recommends friendly harm **downs or wounds, never kills outright**. You explicitly said players could potentially kill a teammate. That's yours to call.

# Art Bible


## Phase 0: Parse Arguments and Context Check


See `.claude/docs/director-gates.md` for the full check pattern. Individual gate definitions live in `.claude/docs/director-gates/[gate-id].md` — the spawned agent reads its own gate file; do not read it in the parent session.


Every `AskUserQuestion` call follows `.claude/docs/automation-modes.md`
(collaborative asks always · guided major-only · autonomous logs and proceeds;
`automation_always_ask` categories always prompt).

**`docs.density`** — it controls per-section *depth*, where `workflow`
controls which sections exist. `modes.rigor` sets both together; set
`docs.density` explicitly to vary depth alone: `terse` (the default, via `rigor: minimal`) = each section a bulleted list of
constraints + references; `balanced` = paragraphs explaining each visual choice
(`rigor: standard`); `thorough` = full prose including style explorations, references, and
rationale per choice. Apply it to every section you author.

**`workflow`** (see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`):
- `full` — all 9 art bible sections required.
- `standard` — required only if visual asset stories exist in the project;
  sections 1–4 are the minimum when required. `workflow_overrides.art_bible_strict:
  true` forces all 9 sections regardless of tier.
- `minimal` — not required. Can still be run voluntarily.

Read `design/gdd/game-concept.md` — or `design/game-brief.md`, the one-page brief
that replaces it at `rigor: minimal`. If neither exists, fail with:
> "No game concept found. Run `/brainstorm` first — the art bible is authored after the game concept is approved."

Extract from game-concept.md (from the brief: working title, pitch, "Who it's for /
what they feel" line and "Art & audio direction" line — it has no pillars, Visual
Identity Anchor or platform):
- Game title (working title)
- Core fantasy and elevator pitch
- Game pillars (all of them)
- **Visual Identity Anchor** section if present (from brainstorm Phase 4 art-director output)
- Target platform (if noted)

**Retrofit mode detection**: Glob `design/art/art-bible.md`. If the file exists,
build the status table **without reading the document** — you are about to author
only the *incomplete* sections, so loading the complete ones is loading exactly
what you will not touch:

```
Grep pattern="^## " path="design/art/art-bible.md" output_mode="content" -n
Grep pattern="\[To be designed\]|\[TBD\]|\[To be written\]|^_?TODO" path="design/art/art-bible.md" output_mode="content" -n
```

- The first grep gives the section headings and their line numbers — the gap
  between consecutive headings is that section's size.
- The second gives placeholder markers and where they fall.
- A section is **Complete** if it has substantive distance to the next heading and
  no placeholder marker inside it; **Placeholder** if a marker falls in its range;
  **Empty** if consecutive headings sit adjacent.
- Where the two greps leave a section genuinely ambiguous, read *that section's*
  line range with `Read(offset, limit)` — never the whole file.
- Build a section status table:

```
Section | Status
--------|--------
1. Visual Identity Statement | [Complete / Empty / Placeholder]
2. Mood & Atmosphere | ...
3. Shape Language | ...
4. Color System | ...
5. Character Design Direction | ...
6. Environment Design Language | ...
7. UI/HUD Visual Direction | ...
8. Asset Standards | ...
9. Reference Direction | ...
```

- Present this table to the user:
  > "Found existing art bible at `design/art/art-bible.md`. [N] sections are complete, [M] need content. I'll work on the incomplete sections only — existing content will not be touched."
- Only work on sections with Status: Empty or Placeholder. Do not re-author sections that are already complete.

If the file does not exist, this is a fresh authoring session. The first
approved section creates the file from `.claude/docs/templates/art-bible.md`,
whose nine `## N. Name` headings are the ones retrofit mode reads — ask first:
"May I create `design/art/art-bible.md` from the art bible template?" Each
approved section then replaces its own `[To be designed]` line with `Edit`;
keep the headings as the template has them.

**A section's approval names its write.** Every section is approved through an
`AskUserQuestion` whose approving option is `[A] Lock this in and write it to
design/art/art-bible.md` (Section 1's full option list is below). Choosing it is
the approval to write that section; no section is written without it, fresh or
retrofit.

Extract performance budgets and the engine for asset standard constraints: read `performance.*` and `engine.name` from `project.yaml`; for any key absent or empty (including when `project.yaml` has no `performance` or `engine` block), fall back to `.claude/docs/technical-preferences.md`.

---

## Phase 1: Framing

Present the session context and ask two questions before authoring anything:

Use `AskUserQuestion` with two tabs:
- Tab **"Scope"** — "Which sections need to be authored today?"
  Options: `Full bible — all 9 sections` / `Visual identity core (sections 1–4 only)` / `Asset standards only (section 8)` / `Resume — fill in missing sections`

  **Mark the option the resolved `workflow` tier actually requires as
  (Recommended), and say why** — the tier already decides this and the user
  should not have to know the tier table to answer:
  - `full` → **Full bible** — all 9 sections are required at this tier.
  - `standard` → **Visual identity core (sections 1–4 only)** — that is the
    documented minimum when an art bible is required at all. Say: "Sections 1–4
    are what `standard` requires; 5–9 are available if you want them."
  - `minimal` → no art bible is required. Say so before asking, and offer
    sections 1–4 as the useful-if-you-want-it option rather than defaulting to 9.
  - `workflow_overrides.art_bible_strict: true` → **Full bible** regardless of tier.

  This is the single biggest cost lever in this skill: every authored section
  carries a specialist spawn, so authoring 9 sections where the tier requires 4
  more than doubles the run for artifacts nothing downstream will check.
- Tab **"References"** — "Do you have reference games, films, or art that define the visual direction?"
  (Free text — let the user type specific titles. Do NOT preset options here.)

If the game-concept.md has a Visual Identity Anchor section, note it:
> "Found a visual identity anchor from brainstorm: '[anchor name] — [one-line rule]'. I'll use this as the foundation for the art bible."

**Author only the sections in the chosen scope.** Phases 2–4 run only the
sections inside it — for `Resume`, the Empty and Placeholder rows of the
retrofit table — and skip every other section, and any phase left with none.
Phase 6 names each section not authored this run and why.

---

## Phase 2: Visual Identity Foundation (Sections 1–4)

These four sections define the core visual language. **All other sections flow from them.** Author and write each to file before moving to the next.

> **Spawn policy for this phase.** Section 1 is delegated on its own — it is
> foundational and the user chooses between anchor directions before anything
> else can build on it. Sections 2–4 are then delegated in **one** `art-director`
> call, not three: they are the same agent receiving the same inputs (Visual
> Identity Statement + pillars), and mood, shape and colour are interdependent —
> an art director defines them together, not in isolation. Three separate calls
> re-sent the same context three times and asked the agent to reason about
> colour without knowing the shape language it had just written.
>
> **This is not reduced specialist involvement** — every section is still
> authored by the specialist, which is the point `.claude/docs/effects-map.md`
> makes about art-bible delegation being mandatory. It is one call instead of
> three for the same three sections. Per-section user approval and
> write-to-file-immediately are unchanged.

### Section 1: Visual Identity Statement

**Goal**: A one-line visual rule plus 2–3 supporting principles that resolve visual ambiguity.

If a visual anchor exists from game-concept.md: present it and ask:
- "Build directly from this anchor?"
- "Revise it before expanding?"
- "Start fresh with new options?"

**Agent delegation (MANDATORY)**: Spawn `art-director` via `Agent`:
- Provide: game concept (elevator pitch, core fantasy), full pillar set, platform target, any reference games/art from Phase 1 framing, the visual anchor if it exists
- Ask: "Draft a Visual Identity Statement for this game. Provide: (1) a one-line visual rule that could resolve any visual decision ambiguity, (2) 2–3 supporting visual principles, each with a one-sentence design test ('when X is ambiguous, this principle says choose Y'). Anchor all principles directly in the stated pillars — each principle must serve a specific pillar.   ---
  
  **Direction: *What You Light, You Can Read***
  
  ### The Rule
  
  > **Light is a resource you spend. Inside it, every machine states its condition. Outside it, the dark is honest.**
  
  **How to use it.** When two visual choices both seem fine, ask three questions in order. The first answer that separates them decides the choice.
  1. Does one of them make the player *spend* something (light, power, attention) to learn what they see?
  2. Does one of them put the information *in the world* (a moving part, a medium, a trail) instead of on top of it?
  3. If the player is lied to here, will the lie leak the sane palette?
  
  **Why this works as a tie-breaker.** It is one sentence with three clauses that map to three kinds of decision: lighting, state display, and truth. Almost every art question lands in one of those. It also keeps the art workload honest. The main cost sits in the 2D lighting pipeline rather than in sprite-state count, so the rule favors cheap, systemic answers (a light, a hue, a trail) over expensive bespoke ones (a new animation per state).
  
  **Alternatives considered.**
  - *"The Dark Is the Default"* alone. It gives strong mood but nothing to say about how a lit machine should look, so it would leave the Satisfactory-style legibility to chance.
  - *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).
  - The hybrid keeps both. Legibility is the reward and darkness is the price.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 1: Darkness Is Honest; Light Is a Decision
  **Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).
  
  Rooms are not fogged, they are *unlit*. Geometry always exists, and any source reveals it exactly as it is. The visible-world edge is the real edge of a real light, never a mask. The physical radius your light actually reveals is a fixed anchor and never lies. Even at low sanity, the hallucination layer may add things but may not move that boundary.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 1 says the physical world is ground truth and only instruments and perception can be wrong. A vignette or fog-of-war mask is an interface lying about the world, and it would give the sanity system nothing to betray. True occlusion gives the player a reliable baseline. A hallucinated shadow with no occluder is then frightening *because* occlusion is normally trustworthy. It also makes light a decision, since each lamp is a visible cost with a visible reach.
  
  **Design test.** When a vignette or fog-of-war mask competes with true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff, choose the true occlusion.
  
  **Alternative rejected.** A soft ambient-reveal radius around the player. It is cheaper to build and reads well, but it makes the player the light source for free, which erases the spend-light economy.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 2: Inside the Light, State Lives in the Sprite, Not the Icon
  **Serves Pillar 2, Dread Before Chaos** (and Pillar 1, since the physical world carries the truth).
  
  Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (a rotor, a fluid, a filament). Failure renders as a trail in the loop's own hue: puddle, frost, scorch, mist, drip. A trail is also a tell. Every breach is preceded by a perceivable escalation, and that escalation is drawn *in the world*, so a careful player can read it. Hue coding is always redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) so it stays readable for colorblind players.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 2 needs tells a careful player could have caught. A banner is read once and dismissed, but a frosting elbow can be seen to worsen from across the room. This is the Satisfactory lesson: watching a machine work is its own reward, and failure can be diagnosed by following the eye along the pipe. Resource loops keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O2 cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey), so a hue is a vocabulary the player learns once.
  
  **Design test.** When a status LED or a "COOLANT LOW" banner competes with a turning rotor with visible fluid or a frosted elbow with a drip, choose the rotor and the elbow.
  
  **Alternatives rejected.**
  - A world-space icon layer on every system. It is cheap, but it reads as an interface and it gives the hallucination system an easy, un-physical target.
  - Heavy per-state sprite sets. They are too expensive for a solo developer, so state should come from shared hue, trail and motion systems instead.
  
  ---
  
  ### Principle 3: Emission Is Exposure
  **Serves Pillar 3, The Web Watches.**
  
  Running loops glow in their own hue. With power off, the ship is lit only by what is still running. Every loop you run is a lantern the web can see. The web itself has no hue of its own and appears only in your light, as oily iridescence under direct illumination. Deeper rings do not change hue. They lower ambient light and raise the iridescence.
  
  **Rationale.** Pillar 3 says Attention is shown in the world, never as a hidden meter, and that restraint is a real strategy. Making light, power use and visibility the *same thing visually* means going dark is a legible tactical choice, not a menu setting. Tying the web's appearance to the player's own light also makes the web's presence feel like a consequence of the player's choices, which supports the "dread is feeling it come" hinge. Keeping hue constant across depth keeps the loop vocabulary from Principle 2 reliable at every ring. Depth is expressed only through ambient and iridescence.
  
  **Design test.** When an on-screen attention meter competes with more filaments resolving in the player's light cone as Attention rises, choose the filaments.
  
  **Alternative rejected.** Shifting the palette per depth ring. It gives strong depth identity, but it would break the flow-coded hue vocabulary, and it would compete with the violet and flesh-tone rule below.
  
  ---
  
  ### Corollary: When the Game Lies, the Lie Leaks (serves Pillar 4)
  
  This is a binding constraint on Pillar 4's hallucination classes, not a fourth principle.
  
  - **Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world.** When either appears, it is the player's sanity and never the location. Every hallucination leaks them somewhere: a fringe, a flicker, a tint at the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
  - **Drift order.** Instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the ship), then the light lies (the cone seems to reach further than it does, shadows with no occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at pipe edges and flesh tones enter.
  - **Anchors that never shift.** Character sprites, hand tools, the HUD frame, and the true light radius. A crewmate's own light beam (colour and shape) also stays truthful, per Pillar 1's human channel.
  
  **Design test.** When a hallucination is perfectly seamless and a hallucination leaks the sane palette, choose the leak.
  
  ---
  
  ### Constraint Notes
  
  - **Art style.** HD pixel art at 3/4 oblique top-down, with Godot 4.7.2 2D lighting. Readability under light comes from silhouette, hue and motion, not from texture noise. This keeps sprites cheap to author and keeps the lighting doing the visual work.
  - **Pipeline consequence.** The lighting-budget spike (a lighting test on D3D12) is the *first* spike, because all three principles depend on 2D lights, occlusion and emission being affordable.
  - **Open for the technical artist.** Whether true occlusion at hard falloff, many emissive loops, and a per-client hallucination filter all fit the lighting budget is unmeasured.   ### Reference Touchstones
  
  - **Project Zomboid.** Lived-in detail and a dark world that you move through at a patient pace.
  - **Satisfactory.** Legible machinery and flows you can read at a glance.
  - **Stellaris.** Dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes.
  - **Barotrauma.** A 2D hostile vessel, with failure you can see happening.
  - **Beyond the Aquila Rift.** A kind-looking lie, where the wrongness is in what leaks through.
  - **Pandorum.** Waking into wrongness aboard a derelict.
  
  ### Checklist
  
  For any new asset or visual feature, answer these before approval.
  1. Does it make the player spend light to see it (Principle 1)?
  2. Does its state live in a moving part or a trail, not an icon (Principle 2)?
  3. If it glows, is that glow exposure, and does it carry the right hue (Principle 3)?
  4. Does it avoid violet and flesh tones in the sane world (Corollary)?
  5. If it is an anchor (character sprite, hand tool, HUD frame, light radius), does it stay unshifted under hallucination (Corollary)?
  
  ---
  
  Notes for the caller:
  - I kept exactly three principles, as in the locked anchor. The sanity/leak rule and the anchors list are a Corollary tied to Pillar 4, so Pillar 4 is covered without adding a fourth principle. Merge it into the principles if you prefer a strict count.
  - Pillar mapping differs slightly from the anchor's implicit order: P1 serves Pillar 1, P2 serves Pillar 2 (plus Pillar 1), P3 serves Pillar 3. Wording was tightened, meaning unchanged.
  - I have not verified how the lighting budget, true occlusion and emission interact in Godot 4.7.2. Treat the "Open for the technical artist" note as a real open item until the first spike answers it.
  - The Corollary's design test line is worded a bit awkwardly ("a hallucination is perfectly seamless and a hallucination leaks..."); consider rewording to "seamless hallucination vs. one that leaks the sane palette -> the leak" when pasting.

**Direction: *What You Light, You Can Read***

### The Rule

> **Light is a resource you spend. Inside it, every machine states its condition. Outside it, the dark is honest.**

**How to use it.** When two visual choices both seem fine, ask three questions in order. The first answer that separates them decides the choice.
1. Does one of them make the player *spend* something (light, power, attention) to learn what they see?
2. Does one of them put the information *in the world* (a moving part, a medium, a trail) instead of on top of it?
3. If the player is lied to here, will the lie leak the sane palette?

**Why this works as a tie-breaker.** It is one sentence with three clauses that map to three kinds of decision: lighting, state display, and truth. Almost every art question lands in one of those. It also keeps the art workload honest. The main cost sits in the 2D lighting pipeline rather than in sprite-state count, so the rule favors cheap, systemic answers (a light, a hue, a trail) over expensive bespoke ones (a new animation per state).

**Alternatives considered.**
- *"The Dark Is the Default"* alone. It gives strong mood but nothing to say about how a lit machine should look, so it would leave the Satisfactory-style legibility to chance.
- *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).
- The hybrid keeps both. Legibility is the reward and darkness is the price.

### Principle 1: Darkness Is Honest; Light Is a Decision
**Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).

Rooms are not fogged, they are *unlit*. Geometry always exists, and any source reveals it exactly as it is. The visible-world edge is the real edge of a real light, never a mask. The physical radius your light actually reveals is a fixed anchor and never lies. Even at low sanity, the hallucination layer may add things but may not move that boundary.

**Rationale.** Pillar 1 says the physical world is ground truth and only instruments and perception can be wrong. A vignette or fog-of-war mask is an interface lying about the world, and it would give the sanity system nothing to betray. True occlusion gives the player a reliable baseline. A hallucinated shadow with no occluder is then frightening *because* occlusion is normally trustworthy. It also makes light a decision, since each lamp is a visible cost with a visible reach.

**Design test.** When a vignette or fog-of-war mask competes with true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff, choose the true occlusion.

**Alternative rejected.** A soft ambient-reveal radius around the player. It is cheaper to build and reads well, but it makes the player the light source for free, which erases the spend-light economy.

### Principle 2: Inside the Light, State Lives in the Sprite, Not the Icon
**Serves Pillar 2, Dread Before Chaos** (and Pillar 1, since the physical world carries the truth).

Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (a rotor, a fluid, a filament). Failure renders as a trail in the loop's own hue: puddle, frost, scorch, mist, drip. A trail is also a tell. Every breach is preceded by a perceivable escalation, and that escalation is drawn *in the world*, so a careful player can read it. Hue coding is always redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) so it stays readable for colorblind players.

**Rationale.** Pillar 2 needs tells a careful player could have caught. A banner is read once and dismissed, but a frosting elbow can be seen to worsen from across the room. This is the Satisfactory lesson: watching a machine work is its own reward, and failure can be diagnosed by following the eye along the pipe. Resource loops keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O₂ cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey), so a hue is a vocabulary the player learns once.

**Design test.** When a status LED or a "COOLANT LOW" banner competes with a turning rotor with visible fluid or a frosted elbow with a drip, choose the rotor and the elbow.

**Alternatives rejected.**
- A world-space icon layer on every system. It is cheap, but it reads as an interface and it gives the hallucination system an easy, un-physical target.
- Heavy per-state sprite sets. They are too expensive for a solo developer, so state should come from shared hue, trail and motion systems instead.

### Principle 3: Emission Is Exposure
**Serves Pillar 3, The Web Watches.**

Running loops glow in their own hue. With power off, the ship is lit only by what is still running. Every loop you run is a lantern the web can see. The web itself has no hue of its own and appears only in your light, as oily iridescence under direct illumination. Deeper rings do not change hue. They lower ambient light and raise the iridescence.

**Rationale.** Pillar 3 says Attention is shown in the world, never as a hidden meter, and that restraint is a real strategy. Making light, power use and visibility the *same thing visually* means going dark is a legible tactical choice, not a menu setting. Tying the web's appearance to the player's own light also makes the web's presence feel like a consequence of the player's choices, which supports the "dread is feeling it come" hinge. Keeping hue constant across depth keeps the loop vocabulary from Principle 2 reliable at every ring. Depth is expressed only through ambient and iridescence.

**Design test.** When an on-screen attention meter competes with more filaments resolving in the player's light cone as Attention rises, choose the filaments.

**Alternative rejected.** Shifting the palette per depth ring. It gives strong depth identity, but it would break the flow-coded hue vocabulary, and it would compete with the violet and flesh-tone rule below.

### Corollary: When the Game Lies, the Lie Leaks (serves Pillar 4)

This is a binding constraint on Pillar 4's hallucination classes, not a fourth principle.

- **Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world.** When either appears, it is the player's sanity and never the location. Every hallucination leaks them somewhere: a fringe, a flicker, a tint at the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
- **Drift order.** Instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the ship), then the light lies (the cone seems to reach further than it does, shadows with no occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at pipe edges and flesh tones enter.
- **Anchors that never shift.** Character sprites, hand tools, the HUD frame, and the true light radius. A crewmate's own light beam (colour and shape) also stays truthful, per Pillar 1's human channel.

**Design test.** A seamless hallucination vs. one that leaks the sane palette → the leak.

### Constraint Notes

- **Art style.** HD pixel art at 3/4 oblique top-down, with Godot 4.7.2 2D lighting. Readability under light comes from silhouette, hue and motion, not from texture noise. This keeps sprites cheap to author and keeps the lighting doing the visual work.
- **Pipeline consequence.** The lighting-budget spike (a lighting test on D3D12) is the *first* spike, because all three principles depend on 2D lights, occlusion and emission being affordable.
- **Open for the technical artist.** Whether true occlusion at hard falloff, many emissive loops, and a per-client hallucination filter all fit the lighting budget is unmeasured. If they don't, the first thing to cut is the number of simultaneous emitters, not the occlusion rule in Principle 1.

### Reference Touchstones

- **Project Zomboid.** Lived-in detail and a dark world that you move through at a patient pace.
- **Satisfactory.** Legible machinery and flows you can read at a glance.
- **Stellaris.** Dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes.
- **Barotrauma.** A 2D hostile vessel, with failure you can see happening.
- **Beyond the Aquila Rift.** A kind-looking lie, where the wrongness is in what leaks through.
- **Pandorum.** Waking into wrongness aboard a derelict.

### Checklist

For any new asset or visual feature, answer these before approval.
1. Does it make the player spend light to see it (Principle 1)?
2. Does its state live in a moving part or a trail, not an icon (Principle 2)?
3. If it glows, is that glow exposure, and does it carry the right hue (Principle 3)?
4. Does it avoid violet and flesh tones in the sane world (Corollary)?
5. If it is an anchor (character sprite, hand tool, HUD frame, light radius), does it stay unshifted under hallucination (Corollary)?
EOF

pat=re.compile(r'(## 1\. Visual Identity Statement\n\n)\[To be designed\].*?(?=\n## 2\.)',re.S)
assert pat.search(s)
s=pat.sub(lambda m:m.group(1)+body+'\n',s)
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s); print("section 1 written")
EOF

**Direction: *What You Light, You Can Read***

### The Rule

> **Light is a resource you spend. Inside it, every machine states its condition. Outside it, the dark is honest.**

**How to use it.** When two visual choices both seem fine, ask three questions in order. The first answer that separates them decides the choice.
1. Does one of them make the player *spend* something (light, power, attention) to learn what they see?
2. Does one of them put the information *in the world* (a moving part, a medium, a trail) instead of on top of it?
3. If the player is lied to here, will the lie leak the sane palette?

**Why this works as a tie-breaker.** It is one sentence with three clauses that map to three kinds of decision: lighting, state display, and truth. Almost every art question lands in one of those. It also keeps the art workload honest. The main cost sits in the 2D lighting pipeline rather than in sprite-state count, so the rule favors cheap, systemic answers (a light, a hue, a trail) over expensive bespoke ones (a new animation per state).

**Alternatives considered.**
- *"The Dark Is the Default"* alone. It gives strong mood but nothing to say about how a lit machine should look, so it would leave the Satisfactory-style legibility to chance.
- *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).
- The hybrid keeps both. Legibility is the reward and darkness is the price.

### Principle 1: Darkness Is Honest; Light Is a Decision
**Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).

Rooms are not fogged, they are *unlit*. Geometry always exists, and any source reveals it exactly as it is. The visible-world edge is the real edge of a real light, never a mask. The physical radius your light actually reveals is a fixed anchor and never lies. Even at low sanity, the hallucination layer may add things but may not move that boundary.

**Rationale.** Pillar 1 says the physical world is ground truth and only instruments and perception can be wrong. A vignette or fog-of-war mask is an interface lying about the world, and it would give the sanity system nothing to betray. True occlusion gives the player a reliable baseline. A hallucinated shadow with no occluder is then frightening *because* occlusion is normally trustworthy. It also makes light a decision, since each lamp is a visible cost with a visible reach.

**Design test.** When a vignette or fog-of-war mask competes with true 2D occlusion from light sources with hard falloff, choose the true occlusion.

**Alternative rejected.** A soft ambient-reveal radius around the player. It is cheaper to build and reads well, but it makes the player the light source for free, which erases the spend-light economy.

### Principle 2: Inside the Light, State Lives in the Sprite, Not the Icon
**Serves Pillar 2, Dread Before Chaos** (and Pillar 1, since the physical world carries the truth).

Every system has a visible moving part and a visible medium (a rotor, a fluid, a filament). Failure renders as a trail in the loop's own hue: puddle, frost, scorch, mist, drip. A trail is also a tell. Every breach is preceded by a perceivable escalation, and that escalation is drawn *in the world*, so a careful player can read it. Hue coding is always redundant with shape and pattern (flow chevrons, pipe diameter) so it stays readable for colorblind players.

**Rationale.** Pillar 2 needs tells a careful player could have caught. A banner is read once and dismissed, but a frosting elbow can be seen to worsen from across the room. This is the Satisfactory lesson: watching a machine work is its own reward, and failure can be diagnosed by following the eye along the pipe. Resource loops keep their hue everywhere they appear (working proposal: O₂ cyan, power amber, coolant ice-blue, fuel orange-red, integrity neutral grey), so a hue is a vocabulary the player learns once.

**Design test.** When a status LED or a "COOLANT LOW" banner competes with a turning rotor with visible fluid or a frosted elbow with a drip, choose the rotor and the elbow.

**Alternatives rejected.**
- A world-space icon layer on every system. It is cheap, but it reads as an interface and it gives the hallucination system an easy, un-physical target.
- Heavy per-state sprite sets. They are too expensive for a solo developer, so state should come from shared hue, trail and motion systems instead.

### Principle 3: Emission Is Exposure
**Serves Pillar 3, The Web Watches.**

Running loops glow in their own hue. With power off, the ship is lit only by what is still running. Every loop you run is a lantern the web can see. The web itself has no hue of its own and appears only in your light, as oily iridescence under direct illumination. Deeper rings do not change hue. They lower ambient light and raise the iridescence.

**Rationale.** Pillar 3 says Attention is shown in the world, never as a hidden meter, and that restraint is a real strategy. Making light, power use and visibility the *same thing visually* means going dark is a legible tactical choice, not a menu setting. Tying the web's appearance to the player's own light also makes the web's presence feel like a consequence of the player's choices, which supports the "dread is feeling it come" hinge. Keeping hue constant across depth keeps the loop vocabulary from Principle 2 reliable at every ring. Depth is expressed only through ambient and iridescence.

**Design test.** When an on-screen attention meter competes with more filaments resolving in the player's light cone as Attention rises, choose the filaments.

**Alternative rejected.** Shifting the palette per depth ring. It gives strong depth identity, but it would break the flow-coded hue vocabulary, and it would compete with the violet and flesh-tone rule below.

### Corollary: When the Game Lies, the Lie Leaks (serves Pillar 4)

This is a binding constraint on Pillar 4's hallucination classes, not a fourth principle.

- **Flesh tones and violet exist nowhere in the sane world.** When either appears, it is the player's sanity and never the location. Every hallucination leaks them somewhere: a fringe, a flicker, a tint at the edge of the light. Subtle is allowed; absent is not.
- **Drift order.** Instruments first (needles disagree with the body of the ship), then the light lies (the cone seems to reach further than it does, shadows with no occluder, temperature shifts), then loop hues bleed violet at pipe edges and flesh tones enter.
- **Anchors that never shift.** Character sprites, hand tools, the HUD frame, and the true light radius. A crewmate's own light beam (colour and shape) also stays truthful, per Pillar 1's human channel.

**Design test.** A seamless hallucination vs. one that leaks the sane palette → the leak.

### Constraint Notes

- **Art style.** HD pixel art at 3/4 oblique top-down, with Godot 4.7.2 2D lighting. Readability under light comes from silhouette, hue and motion, not from texture noise. This keeps sprites cheap to author and keeps the lighting doing the visual work.
- **Pipeline consequence.** The lighting-budget spike (a lighting test on D3D12) is the *first* spike, because all three principles depend on 2D lights, occlusion and emission being affordable.
- **Open for the technical artist.** Whether true occlusion at hard falloff, many emissive loops, and a per-client hallucination filter all fit the lighting budget is unmeasured. If they don't, the first thing to cut is the number of simultaneous emitters, not the occlusion rule in Principle 1.

### Reference Touchstones

- **Project Zomboid.** Lived-in detail and a dark world that you move through at a patient pace.
- **Satisfactory.** Legible machinery and flows you can read at a glance.
- **Stellaris.** Dread delivered by systems, not cutscenes.
- **Barotrauma.** A 2D hostile vessel, with failure you can see happening.
- **Beyond the Aquila Rift.** A kind-looking lie, where the wrongness is in what leaks through.
- **Pandorum.** Waking into wrongness aboard a derelict.

### Checklist

For any new asset or visual feature, answer these before approval.
1. Does it make the player spend light to see it (Principle 1)?
2. Does its state live in a moving part or a trail, not an icon (Principle 2)?
3. If it glows, is that glow exposure, and does it carry the right hue (Principle 3)?
4. Does it avoid violet and flesh tones in the sane world (Corollary)?
5. If it is an anchor (character sprite, hand tool, HUD frame, light radius), does it stay unshifted under hallucination (Corollary)?

- *"Every Pipe Is a Sentence"* alone. It gives strong legibility but treats light as free, which would erase Pillar 3 (The Web Watches).

**Serves Pillar 1, The World Never Lies** (Pillar 3 benefits secondarily).

c hue is entered in this table with a named shape backup before it is used in an asset.

---

**Consistency notes.** Six tensions were resolved across the three sections.   **1. Dark-by-default vs frantic-breach readability.** The bible has done most of the work: §4.6 makes the HUD flat, unlit and on a ground darker than world mid-grey so "world emission never competes with UI", and §2.8's readability rule (2–3 s sweep, trails at full saturation, cone brightest) governs the world layer. Three gaps. (a) §3.5 says the beam cone is "always the brightest thing in frame"; Paper White (L*≈89) sits beside the beam core (L*≈92) and HUD text over a lit region is ≈ 1:1, so the HUD layer must be explicitly exempt and never composited over live world without an opaque ground. (b) §3.5 #5 says a trail "must always out-contrast the panel it crosses" with no number; under the red sweep at 1 % ambient that needs a floor. (c) A brightness/gamma slider is the first control a low-vision player reaches for, and it hands out free light, erasing Principle 1's spend-light economy and Pillar 3's exposure. The bible's own structure gives the fix: the web and horrors are drawn only in direct light (§1 P3, §3.2), so raising the *ambient floor* reveals hull geometry (honest and static) and nothing the exposure economy protects.

This is reconcilable with the fiction: the HUD *is* the suit's visor instrument in the home-ship dialect (§3.4), so it is diegetic-in-fiction and screen-space-in-render. Ship-level loop totals, graph overview and the web map may be diegetic stations (the Barotrauma pattern); the ship-keeper role wants somewhere to stand. Attention and own sanity: the bible rejects meters for both (§1 P3 design test; §4.6 "sanity is not a meter"); the concept's Pillar 3 rejects only a *hidden* meter. For sighted players the in-world channel is sufficient by design; for players who cannot resolve the cone-rim filaments the concept's "audio-first" tells must become a requirement (HR-9), and for players who can use neither, an off-by-default indicator is an art-direction fork, not a pillar violation (Decision 1). Two flows are not yet covered anywhere: (i) the boarder away from the ship — if a home-ship loop fails while they are on a derelict, no trail is visible to them; whether they receive telemetry, and whether it is an instrument or an anchor, decides whether HR-3 gains a sixth item. (ii) "Heat" is in the concept's MVP graph (O₂/heat/power) but §3.3 has no heat loop (O₂, Power, Coolant, Fuel, Integrity); whether heat is the coolant loop or a room-temperature P1 consequence decides whether it ever has a gauge.
  
  **3. Lying instruments vs accessibility.** The bible's answer to "how do I know it is lying" is a violet gleam on the glass (§4.4 stage 1; §4.6: "the only violet that ever reaches the screen-space layer"). For a deutan/tritan player violet reads blue or grey; for a low-vision player a gleam on a needle edge is sub-perceptual; for an achromat Violet core and the Graphite-lit bezel are the same lightness (§4.5). The fix is not to make the lie louder but to give it a motion and sound signature under the same "subtle allowed, absent not" rule, and to recognise that the falsification paths these players actually use are the modality-independent ones: physical consequence (Pillar 1 lists "air hisses", i.e. sound), a second instrument, time, a crewmate. The TD's true-value debug overlay must never be exposed as an accessibility feature; it would delete Pillar 4.

(a) Reduced motion: §4.7 names motion as *primary* for Fuel vs Alarm, and loop direction exists only as animated chevrons/dash-pulse, so a reduced-motion toggle must keep direction as static pointing shapes, replace the sweep with a static mark + sound + HUD glyph, and never suppress trail propagation (P1 information). (b) Sound: §4.0 says "most" semantic colours have a cue; for the five loops it must be *all*, with running and failing tones distinct per loop. (c) Filters: a global daltonization/hue-remap shader can push sane colours into the reserved violet/flesh bands or mask the leak; colour-blind support must be shape/pattern emphasis plus per-element alternates entered in §4.7, never a full-frame remap. HD pixel art implies a bitmap font, so UI-scale steps must be integer multiples or the HUD needs a vector face; that is a Section 7 typography decision for art-director, with this UX constraint attached.

Gamepad.** No cursor over diegetic instruments: proximity focus with an interaction volume larger than the sprite, one contextual action, and (because 3/4-oblique gauges are small) a screen-space *mirror card* showing the focused instrument's reading at HUD size. The mirror shows what the instrument shows (same lie, same gleam, same motion tell); it is a magnifier, not a truth channel. Web map: snap-to-node since filaments are off-grid (§3.3). Beam aiming on the right stick; beam shape is identity (§3.2) and must not change with input device. Destructive actions (cut a section) hold-to-confirm. "Partial gamepad" must be enumerated per flow.

Remote crewmate vitals on your HUD would be a class-(b) instrument and would undercut "crewmates are instruments"; not recommended by default. The speaker indicator (name + beam-shape glyph + stripe count), text chat and any world-space ping are human-channel objects and must be declared anchors; text chat and pings are also the human channel for deaf/HoH and no-mic crews.

(§4.7 motion-primary pairs; Pillar 1)
