  # Section B (Player Fantasy) for Command & Simulation Layer: three framings and a recommendation
  
  I read `design/gdd/game-concept.md` (Core Fantasy, Pillars 1–5, Anti-Pillars, Visual Identity Anchor) and `design/gdd/systems-index.md` (rationale item 1, the Relationship analysis note and the TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY block). I wrote no files.
  
  ## Read this before choosing
  
  1. **The index has already sized this GDD.** Rationale item 1 says this system gets "a short technical spec rather than a full player-facing GDD". So Section B should be one short paragraph that says what the system guarantees. It is not a selling point and it should not be padded.
  2. **Claim only what the kernel actually guarantees.** On its own the kernel guarantees three things:
     - there is exactly one authoritative state;
     - presentation can never write to it;
     - every change is an authority-checked request from a named peer.
  
     It does *not* make the truth visible. The Failure & Trail System, Lighting's true reveal radius and Chat/Voice do that. If Section B says "this system makes the frost honest", a reviewer will rightly flag it as borrowed credit. The honest claim is: **this system is why there is only one truth for the honest channels to show.**
  3. **The anchor should be testable at MVP.** MVP is single-player with only hallucination class (b), false system state. Any anchor that needs co-op can't be playtested until VS-B.
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing A: "The Ship Cannot Lie" (one truth under every instrument)
  
  > The player never meets this system. What they meet is a promise it keeps: there is only one ship. A gauge in the scrubber bay can read green while frost climbs the elbow beside it, and the player has to decide which to believe. The answer is always the same, and it is always available. The gauge and the frost both read the same state, and only one of them passed through the player's mind on the way to the screen. Nothing the player sees, hears or imagines can reach back and change what the ship is doing.
  >
  > The anchor moment is in the cryo bay or the first sortie. The player has "fixed" a scrubber and the needle has settled. Then their breath fogs, and they realise the room is still getting colder. The horror is personal: *I am the thing that is broken.* The comfort is structural: *the ship is not.* Each time a player checks and the world turns out to be right, they learn to trust the world more and their own eyes less. That trust is the only thing this system gives the player, and one desync between what the ship shows and what the ship does would break it.
  
  **Pillar text it serves:**
  - P1: *"Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only instruments and perception can be wrong."* and *"A pipe may look fixed, but the room still gets cold, the air still thins, the pressure still drops."*
  - P4(b): *"Broken reads as fixed, fixed as broken; the lie extends from the gauge to the sprite. The physical consequence (P1) stays honest."*
  - The concept's resolution of the P1/P4 tension: *"the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception are what can be wrong. The tension is the game."*
  
  **Strengths:**
  - It is the exact moment the onboarding names: *"watch the gauge agree with the pipe."*
  - It can be tested at MVP.
  - It is precise about what the kernel contributes.
  
  **Weakness:** it says nothing about co-op, which is the second half of this system's reason to exist.
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing B: "If It Has Your Friend's Light, It Is Your Friend" (identity behind every act)
  
  > Every act in the ship has a name attached to it. When a valve turns, a section is welded or a cutter is raised, the ship knows which crew member did it, and it checks whether they were able to. That is why a sane player can never fake the web's violence. Harm to a crewmate is only accepted from someone whose sanity has actually dropped below the threshold. It is also why the human channel is something you can stake your life on: the thing in the corridor with your friend's beam, the amber cone and the three stripes, is your friend.
  >
  > The anchor moment: a crewmate renders as a horror at the end of a corridor. Its beam is the right shape and colour, and the player has to choose whether to lower the cutter. Later, when the crew tells the story, nobody blames the person who swung. The game does not let them, because the ship recorded who was below the line and the web takes the credit.
  
  **Pillar text it serves:**
  - P1 human channel: *"A monster that speaks in your friend's voice, or carries their torch, is your friend."*
  - P4(c): *"harm to a crewmate is only possible while the attacker's sanity is verifiably below threshold, so a sane player cannot fake it."*
  - Anti-Pillar: *"NOT intentional PvP… attributed to the web. Protects relatedness."*
  
  **Strengths:**
  - It gives real meaning to "peer identity on every command from day one".
  - It speaks to Fellowship (aesthetic #3), the dynamic most likely to go wrong under the lethal-harm decision.
  
  **Weaknesses:**
  - It can't be tested until VS-B.
  - It over-credits the kernel. Voice and beam rendering belong to systems 34 and 20, and the harm gate is enforced by Interaction and Sanity. The kernel only carries the identity and the authority check.
  - As the headline it would push a co-op promise to the front of a foundation that ships single-player first (VS-A is the fallback product).
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing C: "The Ship Keeps Breathing Without You Watching" (a steady pulse under the dread)
  
  > The ship is alive because the crew keeps it alive, minute by minute, and the beat of each minute is honest. Air thins at the same rate whether you are looking at the scrubber or not. Frost spreads whether your light is on it or not. Attention rises on its own count, not when the plot needs it. Under the dread is a steady, indifferent pulse. Dread comes from that indifference: the ship's state does not wait for the player and does not perform for them.
  >
  > The anchor moment: the player comes back from a sortie to a home-ship they left stable, and finds the coolant loop has drifted exactly as far as the time they spent away would predict. The failure is fair because it is consistent, and that makes it feel like the player's fault rather than the game's.
  
  **Pillar text it serves:**
  - Core Fantasy: *"The ship is alive because we keep it alive, minute by minute."*
  - P2: *"Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived."*
  - P1 design test: *"a hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe."*
  
  **Strengths:** it honestly reflects the fixed tick.
  
  **Weaknesses:**
  - Determinism and steady time are mostly the Life-Support Graph's job (fill rates, propagation) and Attention's job (tell timing). The kernel only supplies the beat.
  - It is the weakest link to this system's two stated reasons for existing. Treat it as supporting colour, not the frame.
  
  ---
  
  ## Recommendation: Framing A, with one sentence from B
  
  Use Framing A as Section B, and add a single closing sentence that brings in B's guarantee without making it the headline:
  
  > *In co-op, the same rule gives every act a name. A sane crewmate cannot fake the web's violence, and the beam in the corridor belongs to whoever's beam it is.*
  
  **Why:**
  1. **A is the guarantee this system was created for.** The index says the kernel exists so that presentation can never write simulation. A is that rule as a player feels it, and it uses the user's own suggested anchor (the gauge against the frost).
  2. **It holds up at MVP and in VS-A.** MVP tests exactly class (b) against physical consequences, and VS-A is the shippable single-player fallback. A fantasy that only comes true at VS-B would describe a product that may never ship.
  3. **It stays within what the kernel can honestly claim.** "There is one ship, and nothing you perceive can change it" is a promise the kernel itself keeps. The added sentence credits the identity and authority check without claiming voice or beam rendering.
  4. **It turns the risk into a design test.** Building this kind of trust is a matter of consistency: one visible contradiction (a desync, frost that disagrees with the true state) costs every later check. That is a real acceptance criterion for this system and the reason the Debug Overlay exists.
  
  **Trade-off:** B's Fellowship angle drops to a single sentence. That is fine: the full co-op fantasy belongs in Co-op Session & Replication (33) and Chat, Voice & Pings (34), where those systems actually deliver it.
  
  **Tone and language:**
  - Use the concept's voice: short declarative sentences, physical nouns (frost, elbow, needle, breath, beam), and second person or "the player". Model it on "the dark is honest" and "every pipe is a sentence."
  - **Keep these words out of Section B:** tick, authority, peer, server, registry, command, desync. Section A (Overview) and Section C (Detailed Rules) carry those. The one exception is the design test below, where "desync" is the precise term.
  - No adjectives about feel ("satisfying", "seamless"). State what is guaranteed and what moment shows it.
  
  **Design test to put under Section B:**
  - *"If we're debating between letting a presentation-side effect (a hallucination, a light flicker, a UI animation) adjust simulation state for convenience, or routing it through a command, this fantasy says: route it, or don't do it."*
  - *"The fantasy has failed if any player-visible physical consequence ever disagrees with the authoritative state. That is a P1 violation, not a cosmetic bug."*
  
  The A–B–C labels are just this report's names for the options. Swap them for whatever IDs the GDD uses.
  
  **Options for the user:**
  - **A + one sentence from B (Recommended):** the gauge against the frost, with one co-op line. It can be tested at MVP and makes no claim the kernel can't keep, but co-op gets only one line.
  - **A alone:** the tightest single-player framing. Peer identity goes unmentioned until the co-op GDDs.
  - **B as the lead:** a co-op-first trust framing. It speaks most to Fellowship, but it can't be tested until VS-B and over-credits the kernel.
  - **C as the lead:** a fixed-pulse fairness framing. It is honest about the tick but is mostly the Graph's and Attention's fantasy, not this system's.

  # Section C engine-integration input: Command & Simulation Layer (Godot 4.7.2 pinned)
  
  **Sourcing.** I read VERSION.md, networking.md, breaking-changes.md, current-best-practices.md, modules/physics.md and the kernel rationale in systems-index.md (item 1). The installed editor is 4.7.2.stable.mono, so the reference and the editor match. Where the reference is silent I write NOT SOURCEABLE. Everything marked "general Godot practice (unverified against the pin)" comes from my own knowledge. You should verify it against the pinned 4.7 docs before an ADR depends on it.
  
  The reference does NOT cover signals, Resource/ResourceSaver, `var_to_bytes`, autoloads, typed arrays, `_process` vs `_physics_process` semantics, `Engine.physics_ticks_per_second`, or 2D physics interpolation. The Section C GDD should say so, so the ADRs know which claims carry reference backing.
  
  ## 1. Tick
  
  **What the reference says**
  - `_physics_process(delta)` is the idiom shown for movement in physics.md, input.md and navigation.md. Nothing there describes tick rate, catch-up behaviour or ordering.
  - 2D physics is unchanged since 4.3 ("still Godot Physics 2D"). Jolt is a 3D-only change, so it is irrelevant to this 2D project.
  - The only interpolation entry is "3D physics interpolation rearchitected (4.5): moved from RenderingServer to SceneTree." It is 3D-only. NOT SOURCEABLE: 2D physics interpolation status or API on 4.7, and any interaction between interpolation and a moving parent body carrying child characters.
  
  **Constraints for the GDD to record**
  1. The kernel tick must be a fixed step independent of frame rate. It must be the only place simulation state mutates.
  2. Lean: drive the kernel from a single node's `_physics_process`, with the tick rate equal to the project physics rate. The recommendation is general Godot practice, not reference-backed.
     - Physics 2D bodies (ship body, characters inside it) step on that same cadence.
     - Command application, state-block mutation and physics reads then share one ordered timeline. A custom `_process` accumulator would create two clocks (render and physics) that can disagree about ship and character positions.
     - Counter-case: a custom accumulator is justified only if the sim tick rate must differ from the physics rate, or must be pausable or steppable independently. Headless tests can get this independence more cheaply by calling `kernel.step()` directly (see point 6).
  3. Separate the tick function from its driver. `Kernel.step(commands) -> void` is a plain method with no `delta` dependency. A thin Node calls it from `_physics_process`. Tests and a future server then drive it directly.
  4. The kernel must never read wall-clock time or `delta`. Time is the tick index.
  5. Presentation interpolates, because the sim tick and the render rate differ. This is a presentation-side CanvasItem concern. Whether to use the engine's interpolation is an ADR matter; NOT SOURCEABLE for 2D on 4.7.
  6. The ship-body and interior-physics GDD (#12) must state who writes the body transform into the state block and when in the tick order. This is the highest integration risk: characters inside a moving body, with physics results feeding sim state. The Section C GDD should reserve a fixed phase order: commands applied, then domain systems step, then physics reads or writes, then notifications flush. Whether to read physics results back into blocks is an ADR.
  7. Record the tick rate as a single constant in the kernel spec. Changing it later invalidates tuned simulation values and any recorded replays.
  
  ## 2. State blocks as pure data
  
  The reference has nothing on Resource, RefCounted or Dictionary for saving. The following is general practice or reasoning.
  
  | Option | Headless/no scene tree | Typing and versioning | Serialization | Diffing | Main risk |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | Resource subclass (`class_name FooState extends Resource`, `@export` fields) | Works without a tree | Typed fields; a `schema_version` field is easy | `ResourceSaver` writes `.tres`/`.res`, and `var_to_bytes` / JSON need custom handling | Needs a hand-written `to_dict()` or compare | A `.tres` can embed a script path. Renaming a class or moving a file breaks old saves, and loading a file can instantiate scripts. Do not load untrusted saves this way |
  | RefCounted subclass | Works without a tree; lightest | Typed fields | Must write `to_dict()` / `from_dict()` yourself | Same | Hand-written serializers drift from the fields unless tests enforce parity |
  | Dictionary / packed arrays | Trivially headless | Untyped; typos produce silent nulls | `var_to_bytes` / `JSON` direct | Easy | Fields become stringly-typed. A solo developer will find bugs late |
  
  **Recommendation (an ADR picks the final form).**
  - Each block is a typed RefCounted or Resource class with an explicit `to_dict() -> Dictionary` and `from_dict(d)`.
  - The dictionary form carries `schema_version` (int) and uses only JSON-safe primitives, so it works with either `JSON` or `var_to_bytes`.
  - That dictionary is the one canonical interchange form. Save/Load (#25) serializes it. A later sync layer diffs and sends it. Tests assert against it.
  - A block must contain only data: no Node references, no `NodePath`, no signals into the scene tree, and no callbacks. Identity is by integer or StringName ID, never by object reference.
  - Blocks that hold other objects need an explicit copy or deep-copy rule. The reference notes `duplicate_deep()` (4.5+) as the explicit deep copy for nested Resource trees, and says old `duplicate()` behaviour is retained. Do not assume `duplicate()` is deep.
  - A round-trip test per block is mandatory: `from_dict(to_dict(x))` equals `x`.
  - Diffing summary state for sync: define a per-block `summary()` or `diff(prev)` contract at the kernel level now (a cheap hash or dirty-version counter per block), without building the sync. NOT SOURCEABLE: Godot built-in delta-sync of Resources or Dictionaries. MultiplayerSynchronizer replicates node properties, not kernel blocks (see section 4).
  - Packed-array caveat (4.7, sourced): writing one element of a packed array no longer calls the property's setter. A setter that marks a block dirty will NOT fire on `block.arr[i] = v`. Dirty tracking must be explicit in mutation methods, not in property setters.
  - gdUnit4 tests need no scene tree for any of these options. Plain objects and `Kernel.step()` are enough. gdUnit4 reports orphan nodes as exit 101, so a kernel that avoids Nodes also avoids orphan failures.
  
  ## 3. Change notification
  
  **Requirements.**
  - Presentation must be strictly read-only. Subscribers receive values or immutable snapshots and no mutable reference to a block, so they cannot write state even by accident.
  - The per-client Perception Filter (#20) must be able to transform what a given client sees. Players may see false or hallucinated values, so presentation must not read raw truth directly.
  - The Debug Overlay (#26) needs the true values in addition to the filtered ones.
  
  **Options.**
  - **Godot signals.** Simple and idiomatic. Risks: ordering between subscribers is implicit, emission mid-tick lets subscribers see half-applied state, and lambdas capture locals by value (sourced, current-best-practices), so a state flag set inside a lambda is lost. Share state through a reference type if lambdas are used.
  - **Explicit observer registry** (kernel-owned, called at a fixed point). Deterministic order, testable without a tree, and one place to enforce read-only. More code.
  - **Per-tick snapshot diff.** The kernel produces a per-tick change set (block id, version, changed keys) after the tick completes. Presentation and the filter consume it. It matches the future sync summary well. Cost scales with change count if dirty flags are used. A full diff of every block is wasteful.
  
  **Recommendation.**
  - Notifications are queued during the tick and flushed once, after all mutation, in a fixed phase.
  - The unit is a change record (block id, version, changed keys) delivered through a single kernel signal or registry callback. Godot signals are acceptable as the transport if the flush rule holds.
  - Two consumer channels: a true-value channel (Debug Overlay only) and a filtered channel (the Perception Filter reads true state and publishes what a client perceives). Presentation nodes subscribe to the filtered channel only.
  - Guard: presentation scripts never hold a reference to a state block. They receive a copied value or an immutable view, or query a read-only facade. The presentation-writes-only-CanvasItem/Material/Light2D rule from the brief is enforced by review plus a test that scans presentation scripts for kernel mutation calls. Whether this is a lint or convention is an ADR.
  
  ## 4. Future co-op
  
  **What networking.md says (all of it, briefly)**
  - 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 have no relevant API breaks. ENet host and join go through `ENetMultiplayerPeer` and `multiplayer.multiplayer_peer`.
  - The server-authoritative RPC pattern: `@rpc("any_peer", "call_local", "reliable")` for client requests, an `is_server()` check with validation, then a broadcast via an `"authority"` RPC.
  - MultiplayerSpawner replicates nodes. MultiplayerSynchronizer syncs configured properties, with visibility filters for relevancy.
  - `SceneMultiplayer.auth_callback` and `server_relay` exist.
  - Common mistakes listed: client-to-server RPCs need `"any_peer"`; do not trust client data without server-side validation; use `"unreliable"` only for position-like updates; set `set_multiplayer_authority()` on spawned nodes.
  
  **What the kernel must already do (derived, not stated in the reference)**
  1. **Peer ID on every command.** Single-player is peer 1, which matches the systems-index kernel scope. In Godot the host's unique ID is 1 (general knowledge; networking.md does not state it). Command shape is `{peer_id, tick, seq, type, payload}`. Domain systems never read "the local player" as a global; they take `peer_id` from the command.
  2. **One authority check in one place** (the dispatcher), mirroring the sourced rule "validate on the server." Domain code never validates peers itself.
  3. **Deterministic ordering.** Commands are applied in a defined order (tick, then peer ID, then sequence number), never in arrival or dictionary-iteration order. State-block registry iteration is ordered by registration ID.
  4. **Commands are serializable data.** Payloads use only types that RPC or `var_to_bytes` can carry (primitives, packed arrays, StringName/ID). No Node or Object references. Note that Godot's RPC default is to disallow object serialization; the reference does not cover this (NOT SOURCEABLE).
  5. **Summary-state sync, not node-property sync.** MultiplayerSynchronizer replicates node properties. The kernel's blocks are not nodes. A future replication layer would either mirror summary blocks into synchronizer-visible properties on a thin proxy node or ship change records through RPC. The spawner and synchronizer fit the presentation and character nodes. They do not fit the authoritative state blocks directly. NOT SOURCEABLE: bandwidth, interest management or delta behaviour of MultiplayerSynchronizer on 4.7. The kernel must therefore expose `get_summary(block_id)`, `apply_summary(block_id, data)` and per-block version counters now, so the replication layer is additive. Whether this proxy approach is right is an ADR (co-op replication, #33).
  6. **Prediction and reconciliation** (a client applying its own commands speculatively): NOT SOURCEABLE and out of scope for MVP. The only guard now is that commands carry `tick` and `seq`, and that the sim is deterministic for given inputs. Note that floating-point and physics determinism across machines is not guaranteed. The reference claims Jolt is "more deterministic," but Jolt is 3D-only and Godot Physics 2D has no determinism claim. Therefore the GDD should record: do not rely on lockstep determinism of physics; host state is the truth.
  7. No kernel code should call `multiplayer.*`. A single adapter at the edge translates RPCs into commands and change records into sync messages.
  
  ## 5. Hard limits and gotchas from the pinned reference
  
  - **4.7 typed-return overrides (sourced, GDScript breaks):** an override of a method with a typed return type inherits that type and needs an explicit `return` (`return null` fix). This bites abstract-style base classes such as a `StateBlock` base with `func to_dict() -> Dictionary` or a `Command.apply() -> Result` that subclasses override. Every override must return on every path.
  - **4.5 `@abstract` (sourced):** classes and methods can be enforced abstract. An abstract method has no body. Usable for `StateBlock` and `Command` bases. The reference shows it only with `class_name ... extends CharacterBody3D`-style declarations; nothing tests it with RefCounted. Verify with a parse check.
  - **4.5 variadic args (sourced):** `...values: Array` comes last and is typed `Array` or untyped. `values: Variant...` and `...values: Array[int]` do not parse. A rest parameter works in lambdas, so `func(...args)` can connect to a signal of any arity. A lambda with the wrong arity errors at runtime ("expected 1 argument(s), but called with 0").
  - **Lambda capture (sourced):** locals are captured by value, and a lambda cannot reassign an outer local. Mutate a shared reference object.
  - **4.7 packed array element writes (sourced):** see section 2.
  - **4.5 `duplicate_deep()` (sourced):** see section 2.
  - **4.4 `FileAccess.store_*` return `bool` (sourced):** save code should check the return value. Relevant to Save/Load (#25).
  - **4.7 `Object.is_class()` takes `StringName` (sourced).** Minor: matters for block-type dispatch by class name.
  - **Typed arrays, autoloads, signal API changes, Resource saving:** the reference lists no breaking changes for these between 4.4 and 4.7. That means none are listed, not that none exist. NOT SOURCEABLE beyond the migration guides. Autoload caveat (sourced, observed): `--check-only` with `-s` fails on valid code that names an autoload ("Identifier not found"). The reliable parse check is the framework's `godot-parse-check.gd`. Practical consequence: if the kernel is an autoload, scripts that name it fail the quick check, and tests that need the kernel should instantiate it directly rather than through the autoload name.
  - **gdUnit4 on the pin (sourced):** 6.2.x runs on 4.7.2 though 4.7.2 is not yet in its README compatibility list (4.5 to 4.7.1 listed). Run `--import` before the first test run. Exit 101 also means orphan nodes leaked. Fresh `--import` crashed on exit in 3 of 17 runs on 4.7.x; rerun it.
  - **Process note:** "Last verified" for most reference files is 2026-02-12 for 4.4 to 4.6 content, so treat older rows as lower-confidence.
  
  ## 6. The three things most likely built wrong, with guard rails
  
  1. **State leaks into the scene tree (blocks that are Nodes, or blocks holding Node refs or signals to nodes).** For a first-time Godot developer, a Node is the default container, and state ends up on the player, the ship and the HUD.
     - Guard rail: blocks extend RefCounted or Resource, never Node, and contain no object references to nodes.
     - Enforcement: one gdUnit4 suite that constructs every registered block with no scene tree running and round-trips it through `to_dict`/`from_dict`. A block that cannot be built headless fails the suite.
     - Add a registry rule that rejects any block whose dictionary form contains a non-primitive.
  
  2. **Presentation mutating state, or the kernel being bypassed.** Typical shapes: a HUD button changes a block directly, a gameplay script sets a field "just this once", a signal handler writes back to a block.
     - Guard rail: all writes go through `Kernel.submit(command)`. Blocks expose read-only snapshots to presentation. Mutation methods live on the domain system and are called only by command handlers.
     - Enforcement: a test that scans presentation scripts for forbidden calls, plus a code-review checklist item. The brief's CanvasItem/Material/Light2D-only rule is the allow-list.
  
  3. **Ticks and notifications done on the wrong clock or in the wrong order** (mutation in `_process`, signals emitted mid-tick with half-applied state, order depending on dictionary iteration or node order, or the ship-body phase and the sim reading each other inconsistently).
     - Guard rail: a single `step()` entry with a fixed phase order (apply commands, step domain systems, physics sync, flush notifications), a tick index instead of time, and sorted command and block iteration.
     - Enforcement: a determinism test that feeds the same command sequence twice into two fresh kernels and asserts identical `to_dict` for every block and the same change-record sequence. This is also the cheapest test that the later co-op addition stays additive.
  
  **Peer ID plumbing is a fourth near-miss worth a guard**: a command constructor that does not require `peer_id` should not exist. A unit test asserts that every command type refuses to construct without it.
  
  ## Items that become ADRs
  Tick driver and rate; block base type and serialization form; notification transport and the Perception Filter channel split; replication adapter shape (#33); 2D interpolation policy; ship-body phase placement in the tick (with #12); whether kernel is an autoload.
  
  ## Open spec ambiguities to resolve before the GDD is final
  - Sim tick rate versus physics rate: same, or independent?
  - Is the ship body transform authoritative sim state (a block) or a physics result read back?
  - Do commands need to be replayable or recordable (affects whether `tick`/`seq` are mandatory in MVP)?

  # Section B (Player Fantasy) for Command & Simulation Layer: three framings and a recommendation
  
  I read `design/gdd/game-concept.md` (Core Fantasy, Pillars 1–5, Anti-Pillars, Visual Identity Anchor) and `design/gdd/systems-index.md` (rationale item 1, the Relationship analysis note and the TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY block). I wrote no files.
  
  ## Read this before choosing
  
  1. **The index has already sized this GDD.** Rationale item 1 says this system gets "a short technical spec rather than a full player-facing GDD". So Section B should be one short paragraph that says what the system guarantees. It is not a selling point and it should not be padded.
  2. **Claim only what the kernel actually guarantees.** On its own the kernel guarantees three things:
     - there is exactly one authoritative state;
     - presentation can never write to it;
     - every change is an authority-checked request from a named peer.
  
     It does *not* make the truth visible. The Failure & Trail System, Lighting's true reveal radius and Chat/Voice do that. If Section B says "this system makes the frost honest", a reviewer will rightly flag it as borrowed credit. The honest claim is: **this system is why there is only one truth for the honest channels to show.**
  3. **The anchor should be testable at MVP.** MVP is single-player with only hallucination class (b), false system state. Any anchor that needs co-op can't be playtested until VS-B.
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing A: "The Ship Cannot Lie" (one truth under every instrument)
  
  > The player never meets this system. What they meet is a promise it keeps: there is only one ship. A gauge in the scrubber bay can read green while frost climbs the elbow beside it, and the player has to decide which to believe. The answer is always the same, and it is always available. The gauge and the frost both read the same state, and only one of them passed through the player's mind on the way to the screen. Nothing the player sees, hears or imagines can reach back and change what the ship is doing.
  >
  > The anchor moment is in the cryo bay or the first sortie. The player has "fixed" a scrubber and the needle has settled. Then their breath fogs, and they realise the room is still getting colder. The horror is personal: *I am the thing that is broken.* The comfort is structural: *the ship is not.* Each time a player checks and the world turns out to be right, they learn to trust the world more and their own eyes less. That trust is the only thing this system gives the player, and one desync between what the ship shows and what the ship does would break it.
  
  **Pillar text it serves:**
  - P1: *"Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only instruments and perception can be wrong."* and *"A pipe may look fixed, but the room still gets cold, the air still thins, the pressure still drops."*
  - P4(b): *"Broken reads as fixed, fixed as broken; the lie extends from the gauge to the sprite. The physical consequence (P1) stays honest."*
  - The concept's resolution of the P1/P4 tension: *"the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception are what can be wrong. The tension is the game."*
  
  **Strengths:**
  - It is the exact moment the onboarding names: *"watch the gauge agree with the pipe."*
  - It can be tested at MVP.
  - It is precise about what the kernel contributes.
  
  **Weakness:** it says nothing about co-op, which is the second half of this system's reason to exist.
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing B: "If It Has Your Friend's Light, It Is Your Friend" (identity behind every act)
  
  > Every act in the ship has a name attached to it. When a valve turns, a section is welded or a cutter is raised, the ship knows which crew member did it, and it checks whether they were able to. That is why a sane player can never fake the web's violence. Harm to a crewmate is only accepted from someone whose sanity has actually dropped below the threshold. It is also why the human channel is something you can stake your life on: the thing in the corridor with your friend's beam, the amber cone and the three stripes, is your friend.
  >
  > The anchor moment: a crewmate renders as a horror at the end of a corridor. Its beam is the right shape and colour, and the player has to choose whether to lower the cutter. Later, when the crew tells the story, nobody blames the person who swung. The game does not let them, because the ship recorded who was below the line and the web takes the credit.
  
  **Pillar text it serves:**
  - P1 human channel: *"A monster that speaks in your friend's voice, or carries their torch, is your friend."*
  - P4(c): *"harm to a crewmate is only possible while the attacker's sanity is verifiably below threshold, so a sane player cannot fake it."*
  - Anti-Pillar: *"NOT intentional PvP… attributed to the web. Protects relatedness."*
  
  **Strengths:**
  - It gives real meaning to "peer identity on every command from day one".
  - It speaks to Fellowship (aesthetic #3), the dynamic most likely to go wrong under the lethal-harm decision.
  
  **Weaknesses:**
  - It can't be tested until VS-B.
  - It over-credits the kernel. Voice and beam rendering belong to systems 34 and 20, and the harm gate is enforced by Interaction and Sanity. The kernel only carries the identity and the authority check.
  - As the headline it would push a co-op promise to the front of a foundation that ships single-player first (VS-A is the fallback product).
  
  ---
  
  ## Framing C: "The Ship Keeps Breathing Without You Watching" (a steady pulse under the dread)
  
  > The ship is alive because the crew keeps it alive, minute by minute, and the beat of each minute is honest. Air thins at the same rate whether you are looking at the scrubber or not. Frost spreads whether your light is on it or not. Attention rises on its own count, not when the plot needs it. Under the dread is a steady, indifferent pulse. Dread comes from that indifference: the ship's state does not wait for the player and does not perform for them.
  >
  > The anchor moment: the player comes back from a sortie to a home-ship they left stable, and finds the coolant loop has drifted exactly as far as the time they spent away would predict. The failure is fair because it is consistent, and that makes it feel like the player's fault rather than the game's.

  - Core Fantasy: *"The ship is alive because we keep it alive, minute by minute."*
  - P2: *"Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived."*
  - P1 design test: *"a hidden stat vs. a visibly leaking pipe → the pipe."*

  ---

  **Tone and language:**
  - Use the concept's voice: short declarative sentences, physical nouns (frost, elbow, needle, breath, beam), and second person or "the player". Model it on "the dark is honest" and "every pipe is a sentence."
  - **Keep these words out of Section B:** tick, authority, peer, server, registry, command, desync. Section A (Overview) and Section C (Detailed Rules) carry those. The one exception is the design test below, where "desync" is the precise term.
  - No adjectives about feel ("satisfying", "seamless"). State what is guaranteed and what moment shows it.
  
  **Design test to put under Section B:**
  - *"If we're debating between letting a presentation-side effect (a hallucination, a light flicker, a UI animation) adjust simulation state for convenience, or routing it through a command, this fantasy says: route it, or don't do it."*
  - *"The fantasy has failed if any player-visible physical consequence ever disagrees with the authoritative state. That is a P1 violation, not a cosmetic bug."*

  - **B as the lead:** a co-op-first trust framing. It speaks most to Fellowship, but it can't be tested until VS-B and over-credits the kernel.
  - **C as the lead:** a fixed-pulse fairness framing. It is honest about the tick but is mostly the Graph's and Attention's fantasy, not this system's.

  ## 1. Tick
  
  **What the reference says**
  - `_physics_process(delta)` is the idiom shown for movement in physics.md, input.md and navigation.md. Nothing there describes tick rate, catch-up behaviour or ordering.
  - 2D physics is unchanged since 4.3 ("still Godot Physics 2D"). Jolt is a 3D-only change, so it is irrelevant to this 2D project.
  - The only interpolation entry is "3D physics interpolation rearchitected (4.5): moved from RenderingServer to SceneTree." It is 3D-only. NOT SOURCEABLE: 2D physics interpolation status or API on 4.7, and any interaction between interpolation and a moving parent body carrying child characters.
  
  **Constraints for the GDD to record**
  1. The kernel tick must be a fixed step independent of frame rate. It must be the only place simulation state mutates.
  2. Lean: drive the kernel from a single node's `_physics_process`, with the tick rate equal to the project physics rate. The recommendation is general Godot practice, not reference-backed.
     - Physics 2D bodies (ship body, characters inside it) step on that same cadence.
     - Command application, state-block mutation and physics reads then share one ordered timeline. A custom `_process` accumulator would create two clocks (render and physics) that can disagree about ship and character positions.
     - Counter-case: a custom accumulator is justified only if the sim tick rate must differ from the physics rate, or must be pausable or steppable independently. Headless tests can get this independence more cheaply by calling `kernel.step()` directly (see point 6).
  3. Separate the tick function from its driver. `Kernel.step(commands) -> void` is a plain method with no `delta` dependency. A thin Node calls it from `_physics_process`. Tests and a future server then drive it directly.
  4. The kernel must never read wall-clock time or `delta`. Time is the tick index.
  5. Presentation interpolates, because the sim tick and the render rate differ. This is a presentation-side CanvasItem concern. Whether to use the engine's interpolation is an ADR matter; NOT SOURCEABLE for 2D on 4.7.
  6. The ship-body and interior-physics GDD (#12) must state who writes the body transform into the state block and when in the tick order. This is the highest integration risk: characters inside a moving body, with physics results feeding sim state. The Section C GDD should reserve a fixed phase order: commands applied, then domain systems step, then physics reads or writes, then notifications flush. Whether to read physics results back into blocks is an ADR.
  7. Record the tick rate as a single constant in the kernel spec. Changing it later invalidates tuned simulation values and any recorded replays.
  
  ## 2. State blocks as pure data
  
  The reference has nothing on Resource, RefCounted or Dictionary for saving. The following is general practice or reasoning.
  
  | Option | Headless/no scene tree | Typing and versioning | Serialization | Diffing | Main risk |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | Resource subclass (`class_name FooState extends Resource`, `@export` fields) | Works without a tree | Typed fields; a `schema_version` field is easy | `ResourceSaver` writes `.tres`/`.res`, and `var_to_bytes` / JSON need custom handling | Needs a hand-written `to_dict()` or compare | A `.tres` can embed a script path.   | Dictionary / packed arrays | Trivially headless | Untyped; typos produce silent nulls | `var_to_bytes` / `JSON` direct | Easy | Fields become stringly-typed. A solo developer will find bugs late |

  - The dictionary form carries `schema_version` (int) and uses only JSON-safe primitives, so it works with either `JSON` or `var_to_bytes`.

  ## 3. Change notification
  
  **Requirements.**
  - Presentation must be strictly read-only. Subscribers receive values or immutable snapshots and no mutable reference to a block, so they cannot write state even by accident.
  - The per-client Perception Filter (#20) must be able to transform what a given client sees. Players may see false or hallucinated values, so presentation must not read raw truth directly.
  - The Debug Overlay (#26) needs the true values in addition to the filtered ones.

## Player Fantasy

*Indirect — the player never meets this system; they meet a promise it keeps.*

**There is only one ship.** A gauge in the scrubber bay can read green while frost climbs the elbow beside it, and the player has to decide which to believe. The answer is always the same, and it is always available: the gauge and the frost both read the same state, and only one of them passed through the player's mind on the way to the screen. Nothing the player sees, hears or imagines can reach back and change what the ship is doing.

The anchor moment is in the cryo bay or on the first sortie. The player has "fixed" a scrubber and the needle has settled. Then their breath fogs, and they realise the room is still getting colder. The horror is personal: *I am the thing that is broken.* The comfort is structural: *the ship is not.* Each time a player checks and the world turns out to be right, they learn to trust the world more and their own eyes less. That trust is the only thing this system gives the player, and one visible contradiction between what the ship shows and what the ship does would spend it.

In co-op, the same rule gives every act a name. A sane crewmate cannot fake the web's violence, and the beam in the corridor belongs to whoever's beam it is.

**Pillars served.** *The World Never Lies*: "Pipes leak, frost forms, air hisses; the physical world is ground truth. Only instruments and perception can be wrong." *Sanity Rewrites Reality*: "Broken reads as fixed, fixed as broken; the lie extends from the gauge to the sprite. The physical consequence stays honest." The concept's own resolution of their tension — "the physical ship is ground truth; instruments and perception are what can be wrong. The tension is the game" — is what this kernel makes structurally true.

**Design tests.**
- If we are debating whether a presentation-side effect (a hallucination, a light flicker, a UI animation) may adjust simulation state for convenience, or must be routed through a command: route it, or don't do it.
- The fantasy has failed if any player-visible physical consequence ever disagrees with the authoritative state. That is a Pillar 1 violation, not a cosmetic bug — and the reason the Debug Overlay exists.

*What this section does not claim*: the kernel does not make the truth visible. Failure & Trail, Lighting's true reveal radius and the human channel do that. The kernel is why there is only one truth for them to show. (Alternatives considered: a co-op-first "identity behind every act" framing — true but untestable before VS-B and over-credits the kernel; a "steady pulse" fairness framing — honest about the tick but mostly the Graph's and Attention's fantasy.)

# Command & Simulation Layer

> Authoring guidance: .claude/docs/templates/guidance/game-design-document-guide.md (load per-section as you author — do not read entirely).

> **Status**: In Design
> **Author**: user + systems-designer, gameplay-programmer, engine-programmer, creative-director, qa-lead (via /design-system, autonomous)
> **Last Updated**: 2026-10-25
> **Last Verified**: 2026-10-25
> **Implements Pillar**: The World Never Lies (P1 — one authoritative truth); Sanity Rewrites Reality (P4 — perception can never write simulation)

## Summary

[To be designed]

> **Quick reference** — Layer: `Foundation` · Priority: `MVP` · Key deps: `None`

## Overview

The Command & Simulation Layer is the thin kernel every other system of The Synaptic Sea runs inside. It advances the simulation at a fixed tick, accepts every change to the game's state as a **command** carrying the identity of the peer that issued it, checks that peer's authority, validates the command against current state, applies it or rejects it with a reason, and then tells presentation what changed. It owns no domain state of its own: the Life-Support Graph, the ship layout, suit vitals, Attention, sanity and the rest each register their own **state block** with the kernel's registry and define their own command handlers. The kernel's job is to be the one door through which truth changes.

The player never sees this system; they interact with it only through the systems built on it — every weld, every valve turned, every step taken is a command the kernel admitted. It is automatic from the player's point of view and invisible when it works.

It exists for two reasons that are both pillars. First, **The World Never Lies** needs one authoritative truth: if any system could mutate state directly, two readers could disagree about whether a pipe is leaking, and the honest-world promise would be unenforceable. Second, **Sanity Rewrites Reality** needs a wall: the Perception Filter and every other presentation script may *read* simulation state and write only what is drawn, never what is true. The kernel is that wall made structural rather than aspirational, and its registry is also the hook the Save/Load contract and the true-value Debug Overlay hang from. The game would lose, without it, the ability to add co-op later without a rewrite (TD-FEASIBILITY: authority discipline from day one — in single-player the local peer simply *is* the host) and the guarantee that a hallucination can never corrupt the ship.

**Design-level only.** Whether the kernel is an autoload, how commands are encoded, and how change notification is delivered are implementation choices → **becomes an ADR** (authority model). *(Framing: technical infrastructure, no ADR yet to cite, no direct player fantasy — selected as the recommended options for a `Core`/`Foundation` system under `autonomous` automation.)*

To my knowledge, Godot ENet clients get randomly assigned peer IDs per connection and only the host is always 1 (not covered by `networking.md`, so verify). A save keyed by peer ID breaks the second time a guest joins.
     - **(proposal)** Persistent per-player state is keyed by a stable `PlayerId` (a seat). The kernel holds the live `peer_id → PlayerId` binding. In single-player, PlayerId 1 is bound to peer 1.
     - This touches Sanity, Suit, Save/Load and the VS-B Host-Owned World (guest carry-over) system.
  2. **"Presentation never writes" collides with UI that issues commands.** The Chart Table (pick a target) and menus must submit commands on behalf of the player.
     - **(proposal)** Distinguish *render presentation* (no submit access) from *input surfaces* (submit access as the local player's seat). Both are barred from mutating blocks. Needs creative-director and technical-director confirmation that this reading of the rule is intended.
  3. **There is a third subscriber class the constraints don't name: projectors.** Layout data must be projected onto physics shapes and bodies (Ship Section & Layout Data Model, Ship Body). Those are not CanvasItem/Material/Light2D writes. **(proposal)**: a `PROJECTOR` class owned by the block owner. It writes engine-side derived objects only and never writes blocks. Needs a technical-director ruling.
  4. **One-owner-per-block vs atomic multi-block commands.** Weld writes Graph, Layout and Body. Resolved in CR-9: owners expose mutators, and the kernel guarantees atomic apply. This is the single most load-bearing design decision in the kernel.
  5. **The index's "12 dependents" list is incomplete.** Interaction, Attention, and the Ship Section & Layout Data Model all register blocks or commands and so depend on the kernel but don't list it in `Depends On`. Item & Module Database is static definitions and probably needs no kernel edge. The Perception Filter's real kernel edge is as a PRESENTATION subscriber (it lists none today). The Life-Support Graph's edge on Save/Load is satisfied by the registry contract and may be redundant. Recommend an index correction.
  6. **Determinism has to be scoped honestly.** Godot physics is not deterministic and floats are not guaranteed across CPUs. The guarantee is: same build and platform, same command stream, same physics-observation stream gives the same kernel-owned state. Host-authoritative co-op does not need cross-machine lockstep, so this is sufficient (see CR-14).

  ## C.1 Core Rules
  
  ### Vocabulary
  
  - **Tick**: one fixed-step iteration of the authoritative simulation. Tick number `T` is a monotonically increasing integer.
  - **State block**: a named, versioned, single-owner container of domain state, registered with the kernel.
  - **Command**: a serializable request to change state, carrying issuer identity.
  - **Owner**: the domain system that is the only writer of a block's contents.
  - **Read view**: the read-only accessor an owner publishes for a block.
  - **Step hook**: owner-registered code that runs in the derived/propagation phase.
  - **Mode**: HOST (authoritative; the only mode in MVP) or MIRROR (VS-B guest: receives state, runs no authoritative tick). The kernel's public API is identical in both.
  
  ### Rules
  
  **CR-1. Fixed tick, decoupled from frame rate (proposal: 60 Hz).** The simulation advances in steps of exactly `1 / TICK_RATE` seconds of *simulated* time, independent of render frame time.
  
  - All simulation durations are expressed in ticks, never wall-clock seconds (the Attention tell window of 10–30 s is 600–1800 ticks at 60 Hz).
  - The kernel does not read wall-clock time anywhere in the simulation path.
  - *Alternatives considered:*
    - (a) Variable timestep: rejected, because it breaks replay, tests and save equivalence.
    - (b) 30 Hz kernel tick: cheaper, and friendlier to a future network. But it adds up to 33 ms input-to-effect latency and sits at an awkward ratio to Godot's 60 Hz physics tick.
    - (c) 60 Hz kernel tick with per-hook step divisors (chosen): input and physics-adjacent systems run every tick, while the Graph, Attention and Suit vitals run at 10–20 Hz via divisors (CR-3). This costs nothing extra and keeps one clock.
  - Tick-source mechanism (physics callback vs custom accumulator) → ADR.
  
  **CR-2. Tick phase order.** Each tick executes these phases, in this order, to completion, with no interleaving:
  
  | # | Phase | What happens | Who may write blocks |
  |---|-------|--------------|----------------------|
  | P0 | Begin | Tick counter increments; the intake queue is *frozen* (commands arriving now wait for T+1) | nobody |
  | P1 | Intake | Frozen queue sorted by the ordering key (CR-13), truncated to the per-tick budget; overflow stays queued in order | nobody |
  | P2 | Dispatch | For each command in order: authority check → validate → apply or reject (CR-5) | the command handler, inside APPLY only |
  | P3 | Step | Registered step hooks run in fixed declared order; each hook runs when `T mod divisor == offset` | the hook's own block, plus owner-declared public mutators of other blocks (CR-9) |
  | P4 | Commit | Dirty sets finalised; the "tick committed" marker advances; interpolation baseline captured | nobody |
  | P5 | Notify | Batched change notifications delivered to subscribers (CR-10) | nobody (writes disabled) |
  | P6 | Boundary services | If pending: snapshot (Saving), state-change requests, command-log append | the kernel only |
  
     - P2 commands see the effects of earlier P2 commands in the same tick.
     - P3 sees all of P2's effects.
     - Subscribers in P5 and all presentation only ever see the post-P4 state, never a half-applied tick.
  
  **CR-3. Step hooks and ordering.** Domain systems register step hooks with `(hook_id, owner, divisor, offset, after: [hook_ids])`.
  
  - The kernel resolves a total order by topological sort of the declared `after` edges. Ties break by registration order, then hook_id lexicographically.
  - A cycle or an unknown hook_id in `after` is a boot-time failure (CR-6).
  - Sim-to-sim data flow within a tick is "reader declares `after` writer". Example: Suit vitals declare `after: graph.propagate` because they read compartment atmosphere.
  - The order is data, so it is testable and printable (Debug Overlay).
  - Hooks may not call the submit API with PLAYER origin. They may submit SYSTEM-origin commands (CR-4).
  
  **CR-4. Command anatomy and origin.** A command is plain serializable data:
  
  | Field | Meaning |
  |-------|---------|
  | `type` | Registered command type ID (owned by a domain system) |
  | `issuer_peer` | Peer ID, stamped by the kernel's ingress, never taken from payload |
  | `origin` | `PLAYER` or `SYSTEM` (stamped by ingress, never from payload) |
  | `actor` | The entity the command acts as (opaque ID), or none |
  | `seq` | Per-issuer monotonically increasing integer |
  | `payload` | Plain data (primitives, arrays, dictionaries, packed arrays), with no object references, node paths or callables |
  | `queued_tick` | Stamped on enqueue |
  
     - In single-player, the local input adapter is the only ingress, stamping `issuer_peer = 1, origin = PLAYER`. SYSTEM origin is used only by host-side code (step hooks, Save/Load control).
     - **Serializability test:** in debug builds every command is round-tripped through serialization before dispatch, even locally. A command that cannot survive the round trip is a defect. This is the cheapest guarantee that a future RPC ingress needs no command-type rewrites.
     - **Submit is fire-and-forget.** The only return is a result event keyed by `(issuer_peer, seq)` (CR-5). There is no synchronous "did it work" return, because a remote client could never provide one. UI that needs the answer waits for the result event.
  
  **CR-5. Command lifecycle.** Every command passes through these stages and reaches exactly one terminal state with exactly one result event delivered to the issuer (the "exactly-one-result" guarantee):
  
  1. **Issued**: submit called.
  2. **Admission** (at submit, before queueing): kernel state accepts commands (C.2); type registered; queue not full; not a duplicate or out-of-order `seq`; issuer rate limit. Failure goes straight to Rejected.
  3. **Queued**: waits for the next tick's P1.
  4. **Authority check** (P2, kernel):
     - (i) `origin` is in the type's `allowed_origins`;
     - (ii) if the type declares `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER`, the kernel's binding table says `issuer_peer` controls `actor`;
     - (iii) the command's age `T − queued_tick` does not exceed the type's `max_age_ticks`.
  5. **Validate** (P2, owner handler, read-only): the owner's `validate(cmd, read_views)` returns OK or a domain reason code. It must be side-effect free and may not write.
  6. **Apply** (P2, owner handler): `apply(cmd, mutation_scope)`. By contract apply cannot fail once validate passed (CR-9).
  7. **Terminal.** The command ends in exactly one of:
  
  | Terminal state | Meaning |
  |----------------|---------|
  | Applied | Effects are in state as of tick T |
  | Rejected(reason) | No effect |
  | Dropped(reason) | Never evaluated: kernel reload or shutdown flushed it |
  | Superseded | Coalesced away by a newer command of a coalescing type |
  
  **Reject reasons (kernel-defined, closed set):** `NOT_ACCEPTING` (kernel state), `PAUSED`, `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, `QUEUE_FULL`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `DUPLICATE_SEQ`, `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED`, `ACTOR_NOT_OWNED`, `STALE`, `MALFORMED` (fails the payload schema check), `VALIDATION_FAILED(domain_code)`. Domain codes are namespaced strings or ints owned by the registering system, which keeps the kernel from defining other systems' semantics. Reasons are for logs, UI feedback and QA, never for deciding whether the world lies.
  
     - Coalescing: a type may declare `coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK` (movement intents). Edge-triggered inputs (press, release, confirm) must declare `coalesce = NONE` or taps are lost.
     - The kernel never retries a rejected command. Retry is the issuer's decision.
  
  **CR-6. Registration happens at boot, then freezes.** Block registration, command-type registration and hook registration are only legal in Booting. After Booting → Running the registries are immutable until shutdown.
  
  - Registration is an explicit declaration at boot, not discovered via the scene tree.
  - Reason: a frozen registry gives a stable block set for snapshots and a stable hook order for determinism, and means no late registration can surprise a replication adapter.
  - Violations (duplicate IDs, unknown command type in a handler, missing owner) fail boot loudly in all builds.
  
  **CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).**
  
  - **The host is the sole authority.** Only the host's kernel (mode HOST) runs the tick and applies commands. A MIRROR kernel never applies commands.
  - **Who may issue what** is declared per command type by its owner:
    - `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}`.
    - A PLAYER command that acts on an entity requires the issuer to control that entity.
    - SYSTEM commands never arrive from the network. Remote ingress always stamps PLAYER.
  - **Binding table (kernel-held identity data, not domain state):** `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {entity IDs controlled}`. Mutated only through a host-only kernel API called by the session owner (in MVP, a boot step; in VS-B, Co-op Session). It is not saved: sessions rebuild it, since peer IDs are per-session. Alternative considered: Player Controller owns the binding as a state block. Rejected because the kernel can then not authority-check without calling a domain system, and tests of the kernel in isolation need a binding. **(proposal; → ADR)**
  - **Single-player is not a special case.** The local player's input is PLAYER-origin peer 1, acting on an entity that peer 1 is bound to. The authority path is exercised on every command from day one. The TD risk "authority discipline lapsing" is mitigated structurally: there is no way to apply a command without passing the authority stage.
  - The kernel authority-checks *who*; owners validate *whether the world allows it*. The kernel never encodes game rules.
  - **Friendly-harm commands:** the kernel checks only issuer→actor ownership. The "attacker is below the sanity threshold" gate lives in Interaction's validate calling Sanity's query. Any such gate evaluates the *actor's* authoritative sanity from a SIM block, never the victim's or the attacker's perception.
  
  **CR-8. State-block registry contract.** To register, an owner provides:
  
  | Element | Contract |
  |---------|----------|
  | `block_id` | Unique, namespaced (`graph.state`). One owner per ID |
  | `owner` | The registering system; the only party permitted to mutate |
  | `schema_version` | Integer, bumped by the owner on any serialized-shape change |
  | `class` | `SIM` or `PERCEPTION_OUT` (CR-12) |
  | `persist` | bool. false = derived or transient, rebuilt after load |
  | `scope` | `SHARED` or `PER_PLAYER` (keyed by PlayerId). Recorded now for VS-B; unused in MVP |
  | `repl_hint` | `HOST_ONLY`, `SHARED_SUMMARY` or `OWNER_PRIVATE`. Mandatory declaration, unused in MVP, so no block is ever shipped without a decision |
  | `snapshot()` | Returns plain data for *canonical* state only. Pure, deterministic container ordering, no object references (entity references by stable ID), no derived caches |
  | `restore(data, stored_version)` | Replaces the whole block. The owner performs any migration from `stored_version` to current; an unsupported version is a reported failure, never a silent default |
  | `default_state()` | Used when a save lacks the block |
  | `post_restore()` | Called after all blocks restored: resolve cross-block IDs, rebuild derived caches, check invariants |
  | `read_view()` | The read-only accessor handed to other systems and subscribers |
  
     - **Restore order** is dependency order (blocks declare `restore_after`); `post_restore` runs for all blocks only after all `restore` calls complete.
     - **Entity IDs** are allocated by the owning block from a counter stored inside that block. The kernel allocates none.
     - **RNG:** no global `randf()` in simulation. Each system draws from a named stream whose counter state lives in the owner's block; the kernel supplies only a pure stream-derivation helper from `(world_seed, stream_name, counter)`. → Section D / ADR
     - **The kernel's own clock is the one kernel-owned registered block** (`kernel.clock`: tick counter plus world seed): other blocks hold absolute-tick timestamps that must survive a save. It contains no domain facts.
  
  **CR-9. Write discipline and atomicity.**
  
  - A block can be written only by its owner's mutators, and mutators only work inside a `WriteScope` the kernel issues during P2 apply or P3 step. Outside those phases (including in validate, P5 subscribers, and presentation) mutators assert in debug builds and are rejected in release.
  - **Cross-block commands (weld, cut, module install, pod hop):** the handler's `apply` may call *public mutators* that other owners explicitly publish. The kernel guarantees that the whole `apply` is atomic with respect to every other command, hook and snapshot. No tick phase interleaves with it, and one notification batch follows.
  - **Failure model: validate-then-apply, no rollback (chosen).** `validate` must prove everything via read-only queries (for weld: the Graph's pure join-validation query), and `apply` is infallible by contract. A failure inside apply is a *defect*: it moves the kernel to Faulted (C.2) and halts the tick.
    - Alternative considered: copy-on-write rollback of touched blocks. Rejected for MVP (cost, complexity). Revisit if validate/apply drift proves a recurring bug source.
    - Alternative considered: event sourcing, where state is a fold over the command log. Rejected as the primary store (log growth, migration pain). The kernel keeps a bounded command log for diagnostics and replay tests only.
  - In step hooks, effects on other systems take one of two forms: (a) an owner-declared unconditional mutator call (for example, a horror writing a footprint into the Graph's footprint channel); (b) a SYSTEM-origin command, validated by the target owner and processed at T+1 intake when the target may reject. Two paths is a complexity cost I accept; gameplay-programmer may want to collapse it.
  - The kernel enforces *phase*, not *caller*. "Only declared mutators are called by declared callers" is enforced by lint and the control manifest, not at runtime. → ADR
  
  **CR-10. Change notification contract.**
  
     - Notifications are emitted once per tick in P5, after commit, batched per block: `(block_id, tick, change_keys)`.
     - `change_keys` is an owner-supplied set of changed entity or field keys; if more than `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS` changed, it collapses to `ALL`.
     - Notification payloads carry **no state**. Subscribers fetch through the block's read view. This keeps notifications identical whether state arrived by command (HOST) or by replication (MIRROR), so presentation code never changes between modes.
     - **Subscriber classes**, declared at subscribe time:
  
  | Class | May do | Examples |
  |-------|--------|----------|
  | `PRESENTATION` | Read SIM and PERCEPTION_OUT views. Write only CanvasItem/Material/Light2D/particles/audio nodes | Failure & Trail, Instruments, HUD, Lighting, Perception Filter, Audio |
  | `PROJECTOR` | Same reads. Write engine-side derived objects owned by its block owner (physics shapes/bodies). Never writes blocks | Layout→physics projection **(proposal; needs TD ruling)** |
  | `REPLICATION` | Read all views marked for replication; send | Co-op adapter (VS-B) |
  | `DIAGNOSTIC` | Read everything, including kernel internals | Debug Overlay |
  | (none for SIM) | Simulation systems do **not** subscribe to notifications | Sim-to-sim is commands or ordered step reads (CR-3, CR-9) |
  
     - Subscriber handlers run with writes disabled, and are not given the submit API.
     - **Sim never calls presentation.** The flow is always state → notification → presentation. Horror "light disturbance" and Attention flicker are state the Lighting system reads, not calls into Lighting.
     - **Render interpolation:** the kernel exposes `tick_alpha` (fraction of the way to the next tick) and owners that need smooth motion expose previous and current committed values in the read view. → Section D / ADR
  
  **CR-11. Time model for presentation.** Presentation runs at render rate and reads "last committed tick" state. It never causes a tick, and pausing presentation effects (reduced motion) never pauses the sim.
  
  **CR-12. Perception isolation, enforced by block class.**
  
     - `SIM` blocks are readable by simulation code (validate, apply, step hooks) and by presentation.
     - `PERCEPTION_OUT` blocks (Sanity's per-player "what lies to show" output) are *write-only to simulation*: sim code, including the owner's own hooks, obtains no read view of them. Presentation and the replication adapter do.
     - Sanity's friendly-harm gate and drift read the sanity *level* (a SIM block), never the perception block.
     - In debug builds an attempted sim-side read of a PERCEPTION_OUT view asserts. In release it returns nothing.
     - Perception state is `persist = false` by default (reproducible from the sanity level and a seed); Sanity may override.
     - In VS-B, PERCEPTION_OUT is `OWNER_PRIVATE`: it replicates only to the owning peer.
  
  **CR-13. Determinism and ordering guarantees.** The following hold in HOST mode, same build and platform:
  
     - **G1 Order:** commands are applied in ascending `(queued_tick, host_order)` where `host_order` is a host-assigned enqueue index. In single-player this is submission order.
     - **G2 Single timeline:** every command applies at exactly one tick; no command applies partially across ticks.
     - **G3 Replay:** given an initial snapshot, the same command stream (with `queued_tick`s) and the same recorded physics observations, kernel-owned and block state at tick N is identical, compared via a canonical snapshot hash.
     - **G4 Save equivalence:** snapshot at tick T, restore, and continue gives a state identical to uninterrupted play (hash-compared), for `persist` blocks. This is the key regression test for the registry contract.
     - **G5 Exactly-one-result** per command (CR-5).
     - **G6 Atomic ticks:** observers never see a partially applied tick.
     - Physics-derived facts (positions after collision, contact events, raycast results used in step) are *inputs* from the engine. For G3 they must be recorded and replayed, or the replay test excludes physics-coupled blocks. This is a stated limit, not a defect. → ADR
  
  **CR-14. Hard rules (non-negotiable; each should become a lint or test).**
  
     - **H1 No domain state in the kernel.** Kernel-owned data is exactly: tick counter and seed (`kernel.clock`), the command queue, the registries, the peer/binding tables, the command log, kernel state, diagnostics. Any proposed addition fails review unless it is infrastructure.
     - **H2 No kernel-defined domain commands.** The kernel registers no gameplay command types. Its control plane (pause, save/load request, shutdown) is a host-local API, not remote commands. In VS-B a guest's pause or save request is a command defined by Session or Save/Load, validated on the host, which then calls the control API.
     - **H3 One owner per block; writes only via the owner's mutators inside a WriteScope.**
     - **H4 Presentation never writes simulation.** Render presentation gets no submit API and no mutators. Input surfaces (CR-4) submit commands only as the local seat.
     - **H5 No simulation system reads perception state** (CR-12).
     - **H6 Peer identity on every command**, kernel-stamped, never payload-borne.
     - **H7 Everything that crosses the kernel boundary is plain data** (commands, results, snapshots, notifications keys). No Object references, Callables or node paths.
     - **H8 No networking code in MVP.** The only ingress is local input; the only egress is local presentation. No ENet, RPC or Synchronizer usage.
     - **H9 Simulation never reads wall-clock or global RNG.**
     - **H10 Kernel logic is scene-tree independent** (runs headless, testable without a scene). Whether the kernel is an autoload or a node → ADR.
  
  **CR-15. Control plane (host-local, not commands).** `request_pause`, `request_resume`, `request_snapshot`, `request_restore`, `request_shutdown`. Callers are Save/Load, the Chart Table/pause UI (via a host-local call, not a command), and the boot code. Requests are honoured at tick boundaries (P6).
  
  **CR-16. Pause semantics.**
  
     - Paused stops the tick (no P0–P5) but not rendering.
     - While Paused, submit accepts only types flagged `allowed_when_paused` by their owner (menu actions, save, resume); everything else is rejected `PAUSED` immediately rather than queued, so there is no burst on resume.
     - **Pause is single-player only.** In co-op, a menu cannot stop a shared sim: VS-B will treat "pause" as a UI overlay and the kernel state stays Running. This must be settled before the Chart Table GDD, since "pick a target" may be assumed to happen while paused.
     - Pausing does not stop the engine scene tree's process modes. Relationship to scene tree pause → ADR.
  
  **CR-17. Bounds and overload behaviour.**
  
     - Intake budget: at most `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` processed per tick; the remainder wait in FIFO order.
     - Queue capacity: `QUEUE_CAPACITY` total and `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY` per issuer; beyond that, `QUEUE_FULL` at admission. Never silent drop, never unbounded growth.
     - Catch-up: if a frame is late, the kernel runs at most `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` ticks, then lets simulated time lag rather than spiral. A lag counter is exposed to diagnostics.
     - Step overrun: P3 exceeding `STEP_BUDGET_MS` logs a diagnostic naming the slowest hooks. The tick still completes (correctness over frame time).
     - A command older than its type's `max_age_ticks` when reached is rejected `STALE`, so a hitch cannot unleash a second of stale movement intents.
  
  **CR-18. Snapshot semantics (Save/Load and future guest transfer).**
  
     - A snapshot is taken only at a tick boundary (P6), covers all `persist` blocks at the same tick T, and records `(T, per-block schema_version)`.
     - Capture is synchronous and in-memory; the tick does not advance during capture (state Saving). File I/O is Save/Load's concern and happens off the kernel's critical path → ADR.
     - Restore replaces *all* persisted blocks atomically; partial restore is not supported. Failure at any block aborts and leaves the kernel in Faulted with the pre-restore state intact if possible. Save/Load decides user messaging.
     - **VS-B reuse:** with join-in-progress deferred, guests still need the world at session start. The same snapshot/restore contract is the transfer mechanism, so it must be complete and cheap.
  
  ### Alternatives considered, summarised
  
  | Decision | Chosen | Rejected and why |
  |----------|--------|------------------|
  | Tick | 60 Hz fixed + step divisors | Variable timestep (no replay); 30 Hz (latency, ratio to physics) |
  | Command return | Async result event | Synchronous bool (impossible for remote issuers) |
  | Multi-block write | Owner mutators + atomic apply, validate-first | Rollback (cost); event sourcing (migration) |
  | Notification | Batched, key-only, post-commit | Signal-per-write (mid-tick inconsistency, spam); state in payload (differs HOST vs MIRROR) |
  | Authority binding | Kernel-held table | Controller-owned block (kernel can't check without a domain call) |
  | Per-player key | PlayerId | Peer ID (unstable across sessions) |

  ## C.2 States and Transitions
  
  ### Kernel states
  
  | State | Meaning | Tick advancing | Accepts submit |
  |-------|---------|----------------|----------------|
  | `BOOTING` | Registries being populated (CR-6); nothing loaded | No | No (`NOT_ACCEPTING`) |
  | `LOADING` | Restoring a snapshot or building a new-game state (also entered mid-session for reload, including the MVP death-stub reload) | No | No (`NOT_ACCEPTING`) |
  | `RUNNING` | Normal ticking | Yes | Yes |
  | `PAUSED` | Single-player pause | No | Only `allowed_when_paused` types |
  | `SAVING` | Snapshot capture at a tick boundary. Transient: returns to the prior state | No | Queues normally (it is expected to be brief); no tick runs until capture completes |
  | `FAULTED` | Invariant violation, apply failure, restore failure, or boot failure after registration. Not requested by anyone | No | No |
  | `SHUTTING_DOWN` | Teardown | No | No |
  
  `FAULTED` is an addition to the requested list. Without it, an infallible-apply violation (CR-9) has nowhere to go but undefined behaviour. In FAULTED the kernel never writes or autosaves over an existing save. A dev build halts with diagnostics; release returns to the menu.
  
  ### State transitions
  
  | From | Trigger | To | Notes |
  |------|---------|----|-------|
  | (start) | Process start | BOOTING | |
  | BOOTING | Registries valid and frozen | LOADING | A new game also passes through LOADING, populating blocks from `default_state()` |
  | BOOTING | Duplicate ID, hook cycle, unknown dependency | FAULTED | |
  | LOADING | All blocks restored, `post_restore` passes | RUNNING | Initial state is RUNNING (or PAUSED if the caller requested it) |
  | LOADING | Restore or `post_restore` fails | FAULTED | Previous state preserved if possible |
  | RUNNING | `request_pause` | PAUSED | Honoured at the next tick boundary |
  | PAUSED | `request_resume` | RUNNING | |
  | RUNNING / PAUSED | `request_snapshot` | SAVING | Remembers the return state |
  | SAVING | Capture complete | prior state (RUNNING or PAUSED) | |
  | SAVING | Capture error | FAULTED | |
  | RUNNING / PAUSED | `request_restore` (reload, load game, death stub) | LOADING | Queue is flushed; every flushed command receives `Dropped(RELOAD)` |
  | RUNNING / PAUSED / FAULTED | `request_shutdown` | SHUTTING_DOWN | Queue flushed with `Dropped(SHUTDOWN)` |
  | RUNNING | Apply failure, step invariant failure | FAULTED | |
  | FAULTED | `request_restore` (explicit user action) | LOADING | The only way out other than shutdown |
  | SHUTTING_DOWN | Teardown complete | (end) | |
  
  Every other (state, trigger) pair is invalid. The kernel ignores it and reports it to diagnostics. It is never a silent state change. In particular: no transition from SAVING except to its return state or FAULTED; no restore request during SAVING (it waits for the boundary); no RUNNING from BOOTING directly.
  
  ### Per-command states
  
  | State | Entered when | Next |
  |-------|--------------|------|
  | `ISSUED` | submit called | ADMITTED or REJECTED |
  | `ADMITTED` | passes admission | QUEUED |
  | `QUEUED` | enqueued | AUTHORIZING, or DROPPED on reload/shutdown flush, or SUPERSEDED by a coalescing successor |
  | `AUTHORIZING` | reached in P2 | VALIDATING or REJECTED |
  | `VALIDATING` | authority passed | APPLYING or REJECTED |
  | `APPLYING` | validate OK | APPLIED (or kernel FAULTED on apply failure) |
  | `APPLIED` (terminal) | | result event emitted |
  | `REJECTED(reason)` (terminal) | any failing stage | result event emitted |
  | `DROPPED(reason)` (terminal) | flush | result event emitted |
  | `SUPERSEDED` (terminal) | coalesced away | result event emitted |

  ## C.3 Interactions with Other Systems

  **From gameplay-programmer (feel/latency):**

  ---
  
  ## Findings that change the brief (read first)
  
  1. **Peer ID is the wrong key for persistent per-player state.** The index says Sanity writes perception state "keyed by peer ID". To my knowledge, Godot ENet clients get randomly assigned peer IDs per connection and only the host is always 1 (not covered by `networking.md`, so verify). A save keyed by peer ID breaks the second time a guest joins.
     - **(proposal)** Persistent per-player state is keyed by a stable `PlayerId` (a seat). The kernel holds the live `peer_id → PlayerId` binding. In single-player, PlayerId 1 is bound to peer 1.
     - This touches Sanity, Suit, Save/Load and the VS-B Host-Owned World (guest carry-over) system.
  2. **"Presentation never writes" collides with UI that issues commands.** The Chart Table (pick a target) and menus must submit commands on behalf of the player.
     - **(proposal)** Distinguish *render presentation* (no submit access) from *input surfaces* (submit access as the local player's seat). Both are barred from mutating blocks. Needs creative-director and technical-director confirmation that this reading of the rule is intended.
