timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

#
# PURPOSE: Single source of truth for all named game-world facts that appear
# in more than one document. Skills check this before writing new content to
# detect cross-doc inconsistencies at authoring time.
#
# RULES:

#     (a formula used in one GDD only) do NOT need to be registered.
#   - Never delete entries — set status: deprecated instead.
#   - When a value changes: update the value, set revised: to today's date,
#     and add a comment with the old value and which GDD changed it.
#   - source: is the authoritative GDD — the one that "owns" this fact.
#     Other GDDs that reference it list themselves in referenced_by.

"""Apply entry-scoped registry edits from the decide workflow's journal; then un-park pending referenced_by
comments whose files exist. Prints a count line per edit (ok / SKIP(n) / NOENTRY)."""
import json, re, os, sys
ROOT = 'D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d'; Y = f'{ROOT}/design/registry/entities.yaml'
import glob
edits = []
for J in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(glob.glob(J)):
        if f.endswith('.jsonl'):
            L = [json.loads(l) for l in open(f, encoding='utf-8')]
            edits += [e for x in L if x['type'] == 'result' and x['result'] for e in x['result']['edits']]
        else:
            d = json.load(open(f, encoding='utf-8')); edits += d['edits'] if isinstance(d, dict) else d
s = open(Y, encoding='utf-8', newline='').read()
crlf = '\r\n' in s
s = s.replace('\r\n', '\n')
def block(name):
    m = re.search(r'^  - name: "?' + re.escape(name) + r'"?\n', s, re.M)
    if not m: return None
    n = re.search(r'^(  - name: |[a-z_]+:|# )', s[m.end():], re.M)
    return m.start(), (m.end() + n.start()) if n else len(s)
ok = skip = noent = 0
for e in edits:
    b = block(e['name'])
    if not b: print('NOENTRY', e['name']); noent += 1; continue
    i, j = b; blk = s[i:j]; c = blk.count(e['old_text'])
    if c == 1:
        s = s[:i] + blk.replace(e['old_text'], e['new_text'], 1) + s[j:]; ok += 1
    else:
        print(f'SKIP({c})', e['name'], repr(e['old_text'][:70])); skip += 1
# un-park pending referenced_by
up = 0
def unpark(m):
    global up
    paths = [p.strip() for p in m.group(2).split(',') if p.strip()]
    return m.group(0)
out, lines = [], s.split('\n')
for k, l in enumerate(lines):
    m = re.match(r'^(\s*)# pending referenced_by \(GDD not yet written\): (.+)$', l)
    if not m: out.append(l); continue
    paths = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r'[,\s]+', m.group(2)) if p.strip().endswith('.md')]
    exist = [p for p in paths if os.path.exists(f'{ROOT}/{p}')]
    left = [p for p in paths if p not in exist]
    # find referenced_by of this entry (search backwards)
    for q in range(len(out) - 1, -1, -1):
        if out[q].startswith('  - name: '): break
        if re.match(r'^    referenced_by:', out[q]):
            if out[q].strip().endswith('[]'): out[q] = '    referenced_by:'; ins = q + 1
            else:
                ins = q + 1
                while ins < len(out) and out[ins].startswith('      - '): ins += 1
            have = {x.strip()[2:] for x in out[q + 1:ins]}
            new = [f'      - {p}' for p in exist if p not in have]
            out[ins:ins] = new; up += len(exist)
            break
    else:
        left = paths
    if left: out.append(f'{m.group(1)}# pending referenced_by (GDD not yet written): {", ".join(left)}')
s = '\n'.join(out)
if crlf: s = s.replace('\n', '\r\n')
open(Y, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='').write(s)
print(f'edits: {len(edits)} ok {ok} skip {skip} noentry {noent}; unparked paths {up}')

# Design

Work the way the design lead at a small studio would: make deliberate choices about palette, typography and layout that are specific to this subject.

## Read the request first

Every page is designed; decide only the treatment. A memo gets the same craft as a landing page.

- Many requests call for a utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing and a proper palette, but do not over-design: most pages need no flashy, gigantic hero, and few flourishes.
- Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool the user will keep or share. For those, read the editorial topic too.
- If unsure, a well-composed plain page is always acceptable; an over-designed one sometimes is not.

## Before writing

- If the page, the user or their project has a design system, apply it. The user's own words come first, then that system, then your choices.
- Define the subject, its audience and the page's single job. Use real content, never lorem ipsum. Include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament.
- Settle a short plan and write it into the page as the :root block at the top of its <style>: 4 to 6 named color tokens, font tokens for display and body, the layout idea as a one-line comment. Build the rest from those tokens. Unless the user asks about the design, tell them at most one plain sentence on its direction, with no hex values or font names.

## Name

The <title> is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab. Give it a real name that picks this page out among dozens: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, or the question itself for a page that answers one. No explanation after a dash or a colon. When trimming, keep the identifying word, not the generic one. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use it.

## Type

- Pair a display face, used with restraint, with a body face. Link Google Fonts directly; declare a real fallback stack.
- Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it.
- Give headings text-wrap: balance. Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums where digits line up in columns.

## Color and themes

The page renders in the viewer's theme. The viewer sets data-theme="dark" or data-theme="light" on the root element, or nothing at all, in which case only prefers-color-scheme tells light from dark.

- Define the complete light palette as tokens in the bare :root block, before any media or [data-theme] block redefines them; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug.
- Redefine the tokens under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), guarded as :root:not([data-theme="light"]).
- Redefine them again under :root[data-theme="dark"]. Set color-scheme: dark wherever the dark palette applies.
- Style every element through the tokens, never directly inside those blocks.
- Set an explicit background on body from a token. A transparent body shows the host's background.
- Give the second theme the same care: do not simply invert it; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both backgrounds.
- Choose neutrals deliberately: a grey with a slight bias toward the accent reads as intended.
- A page that commits to one visual world may stay single-theme, by choice: omit the media and [data-theme] blocks, and set the background, every color and color-scheme explicitly.

## Layout

- Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and gap, not per-element margins.
- Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width, about 400px.
- Give images max-width: 100%. Only wide tables, code and diagrams may exceed the screen; give each overflow-x: auto on its own container, so the page body never scrolls sideways.
- Size a one-screen app with height: 100% on html and body, not 100vh.
- Make repeated elements consistent: the same edges, baselines and padding on each card or row. Text that outgrows its box wraps or scrolls: clipped text is a bug.
- Use borders, fills, radius and shadow by role, to set off the one element that needs it.

## Complete at rest

Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded: nothing waits for a scroll or a click to appear. That first frame is what a thumbnail and a shared link show. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state, with the user's real data or clearly marked examples, never an empty shell. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at opacity: 0 waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content, not the viewport: a 100vh opener pushes the rest out of that frame.

## Tools and dashboards

These are scanned and operated, not read top to bottom: the craft shifts from typography to information design.

- Put the summary before the detail.
- Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance.
- Semantic color (good, warning, critical) is separate from the accent and does not count as it.
- Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint.
- Interactive elements should look interactive.
- Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

## Libraries and graphics

- Most pages need no library. When one does substantial work, load its UMD build with one <script src> from cdnjs, placed before the inline script that uses it; do not paste its source into the page or write your own version of it. Inline only its stylesheet.
- Pin every library URL to an exact version (react@18.3.1 on jsDelivr or unpkg, react/18.3.1/… on cdnjs, cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17), never a bare name, a range or a tag (react@18, @latest). Choose one at least two weeks old: any you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any from the last two weeks.
- Draw charts to one scale, with every label naming a value the chart reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens. Keep marks and labels clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds.
- For generative or decorative graphics use Canvas, not long hand-written SVG paths.

## Avoid the generic looks

Without a direction from the user, do not fall back on: warm cream with a serif display and a terracotta accent; near-black with one acid-green accent; a purple-to-blue gradient hero; Inter or Space Grotesk as the safe face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; the same rounded card everywhere. When the user asks for one of these, follow them.

## Words

Write from the user's side of the screen. Name things by what people recognize. Use active voice; a control says exactly what happens. Errors say what went wrong and how to fix it. Prefer specific to clever, and short, direct sentences. Avoid mannered devices: em-dash asides, "not X, but Y", colon-then-reveal, scare quotes on invented labels, stock phrases like "worth noting". Numbered markers, eyebrows and dividers must encode something true about the content.

## Build cleanly

Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect prefers-reduced-motion, and give every form control a stable id. Watch selector specificity so one rule does not silently undo another's spacing.

## Write, check once, publish

Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way, such as one screenshot of the file you wrote; otherwise skip the look. Make one pass of edits for what it shows, then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring) may also get one run of a pure function. Never loop, since the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Further polish is for the user to request: if they report something visibly broken, fix that, look at most once more, and republish once.

# Pages

An artifact is a web page this server hosts at a claude.ai link. These are the rules the server applies.

## What a page is

- One complete HTML document. Begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>: content that does not read as HTML is refused. To publish a Markdown document, write an HTML page from its content.
- A page published as one document carries its own CSS, JavaScript, data and images (data: URIs or inline SVG); only the libraries and fonts listed below load from outside. A page published from files may also load its own files by relative path.
- Give it a <title>. On a new artifact pass the same words as title.
- Put viewport-fit=cover in its viewport meta only with env(safe-area-inset-*) padding: the Claude iOS app draws such a page under its top bar.
- A page can be up to 16 MiB.

## What a page may load

The page runs under a content security policy. Apart from the artifact's own files, anything not listed here is blocked by the browser, with no error on the page.

- Scripts: inline, or from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/python-visualization/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com, code.jquery.com, cdn.plot.ly.
- Stylesheets: inline, or from fonts.googleapis.com. A library's stylesheet from any other host must be inlined or shipped as one of the page's own files.
- Fonts: from fonts.gstatic.com (through a Google Fonts stylesheet), or inlined as data: URIs.
- Images and media: data: and blob: URIs. A remote image does not load.
- fetch, XMLHttpRequest and WebSocket to other hosts are blocked.

## What the viewer's frame allows

The page runs in a sandboxed frame.

- Refused or ignored: alert, confirm and prompt; window.print; downloads the page starts, by <a download> or by script; clipboard reads (the viewer's own paste works); camera, microphone, location, motion, screen capture and Web Share; service workers; WebRTC; <object>, <embed> and iframes of other sites. Build dialogs into the page, offer a Copy button where you would offer an export, and offer no button for the others unless a capability (last item) provides it.
- Link to other sites with a plain <a href>, which the viewer opens outside the page; window.open fails for most viewers.
- mailto:, tel: and other non-web links fail for many viewers: keep the link, show the address or number as text too, and never report a message as sent.
- A form has nowhere to submit: handle submit in script, with preventDefault().
- Call these only from a click handler, and catch a refusal: navigator.clipboard.writeText, fullscreen, pointer lock, audio playback.
- These work: file inputs and dropped files (use them in place of the camera and microphone), Web Workers from the page's own files or blob: URLs.
- localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB keep data in one viewer's browser. It survives a republish, reaches no other viewer or device and not Claude, and may be missing or throw: use try/catch and render well without it. Use it only for one viewer's conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, an unsent draft), never for state that must last.
- Only a plain #name passes between the artifact's URL and location.hash, never #/path, #key=value, a pushState path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens such as #costs-emea (never settings, sidebar, customize, upgrade, downloads or comment-*, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in location.hash, or the start view if none, on load and on hashchange. Keep other state in the page, and keys, tokens or private values out of the hash: it shows in history and copied links.
- Where this server lists a tool that describes page capabilities, call it before writing a page that needs downloads, a device, state that must last, or data that other viewers or devices must see: a capability may provide it. If none does, tell the user what cannot work, and do not fake it.

## Who can see it

A new artifact is visible to its owner only. This server cannot change who can see an artifact; the owner shares it from its page on claude.ai.

## Publishing

- Where this server lists a tool that publishes from files on disk and you can write files, that is the way to publish a page you write: write the page to a file in your working folder, then publish the file without stopping to ask, with title and icon. You write the page once, and the file is yours to look at and edit later.
- Where it lists none, where you cannot write files, or where that tool answers that the client cannot attach files: publish_version with title, icon and content, no slug.
- Either way the result carries slug, version and url.
- Small change to a page: edit_version with slug, base_version and edits. The server reads the page, replaces each old_text with its new_text, and publishes the result. Nothing is published if an edit does not apply.
- Small change to another text file of an artifact published from files, such as a stylesheet or a script: the same call with path. Every other file is kept. A JSON file must still parse after the edits, or nothing is published.
- Whole new page for an existing artifact: publish it as you would a new page, adding slug and base_version. Whichever way you publish it, the artifact's other files, if it has any, are kept and still served. A publish from files can also remove the ones the new page no longer uses.
- When the artifact's read value is users, org or public, every republish also passes shared_live with that word. It states who the artifact is already shared with and changes nothing.
- base_version is the version you last saw: from your last publish result, get_artifact or read_artifact. If someone published since, the call is refused with a conflict that names the live version. Do what the refusal's error sentence says. If it has none, read the artifact again, redo the change on the current page, and retry; never retry with the new version and your old content.
- Omit title and icon when republishing to keep them. Pass title only to rename.
- read_artifact reads a page the user owns, or one that belongs to someone in the user's organization and that the user can open. Where it refuses a page because of who has written to it, it names read_shared_artifact, and the user is asked first. A page the user does not own can be republished only with edit_version or publish_version, and only if it is in the user's organization, is not public, and the user can edit it.
- To read a page too large for one result, call read_artifact with offset and follow next_offset. A part is never the whole page: do not send it to publish_version.
- After a publish, say in one sentence what the page is, or what changed on a republish, and give the user the url. If your instructions or the publish result say the user's app already shows a card with the page's link, leave the url out unless the user asks for it.
- The published page is the delivery. If you wrote a file, keep it, but do not also send it to the user unless they ask for it.

## What is refused

- Artifacts of another organization, and ones the user does not own and cannot edit.
- Public artifacts the user does not own.
- By publish_version, and by edit_version without path: artifacts made from a type (a slide deck, a document, a design). Where this server offers a tool that publishes from files, it publishes the content files of one whose type keeps content in files, in patch mode, and edit_version with path replaces text in one of them; the type's own files cannot be changed.
- Artifacts that hold a live document.
- Content that is not HTML, or that embeds an archive or a PDF.

# Design

Work the way the design lead at a small studio would: make deliberate choices about palette, typography and layout that are specific to this subject.

## Read the request first

Every page is designed; decide only the treatment. A memo gets the same craft as a landing page.

- Many requests call for a utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing and a proper palette, but do not over-design: most pages need no flashy, gigantic hero, and few flourishes.
- Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool the user will keep or share. For those, read the editorial topic too.
- If unsure, a well-composed plain page is always acceptable; an over-designed one sometimes is not.

## Before writing

- If the page, the user or their project has a design system, apply it. The user's own words come first, then that system, then your choices.

- Settle a short plan and write it into the page as the :root block at the top of its <style>: 4 to 6 named color tokens, font tokens for display and body, the layout idea as a one-line comment. The <title> is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab. - Pair a display face, used with restraint, with a body face. Link Google Fonts directly; declare a real fallback stack.

content.text:
# Pages

An artifact is a web page this server hosts at a claude.ai link. These are the rules the server applies.

## What a page is

- One complete HTML document. Begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>: content that does not read as HTML is refused. To publish a Markdown document, write an HTML page from its content.
- A page published as one document carries its own CSS, JavaScript, data and images (data: URIs or inline SVG); only the libraries and fonts listed below load from outside. A page published from files may also load its own files by relative path.
- Give it a <title>. On a new artifact pass the same words as title.
- Put viewport-fit=cover in its viewport meta only with env(safe-area-inset-*) padding: the Claude iOS app draws such a page under its top bar.
- A page can be up to 16 MiB.

## What a page may load

The page runs under a content security policy. Apart from the artifact's own files, anything not listed here is blocked by the browser, with no error on the page.

- Scripts: inline, or from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/python-visualization/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com, code.jquery.com, cdn.plot.ly.
- Stylesheets: inline, or from fonts.googleapis.com. A library's stylesheet from any other host must be inlined or shipped as one of the page's own files.
- Fonts: from fonts.gstatic.com (through a Google Fonts stylesheet), or inlined as data: URIs.
- Images and media: data: and blob: URIs. A remote image does not load.
- fetch, XMLHttpRequest and WebSocket to other hosts are blocked.

## What the viewer's frame allows

The page runs in a sandboxed frame.

- Refused or ignored: alert, confirm and prompt; window.print; downloads the page starts, by <a download> or by script; clipboard reads (the viewer's own paste works); camera, microphone, location, motion, screen capture and Web Share; service workers; WebRTC; <object>, <embed> and iframes of other sites. Build dialogs into the page, offer a Copy button where you would offer an export, and offer no button for the others unless a capability (last item) provides it.
- Link to other sites with a plain <a href>, which the viewer opens outside the page; window.open fails for most viewers.
- mailto:, tel: and other non-web links fail for many viewers: keep the link, show the address or number as text too, and never report a message as sent.
- A form has nowhere to submit: handle submit in script, with preventDefault().
- Call these only from a click handler, and catch a refusal: navigator.clipboard.writeText, fullscreen, pointer lock, audio playback.
- These work: file inputs and dropped files (use them in place of the camera and microphone), Web Workers from the page's own files or blob: URLs.
- localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB keep data in one viewer's browser. It survives a republish, reaches no other viewer or device and not Claude, and may be missing or throw: use try/catch and render well without it. Use it only for one viewer's conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, an unsent draft), never for state that must last.
- Only a plain #name passes between the artifact's URL and location.hash, never #/path, #key=value, a pushState path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens such as #costs-emea (never settings, sidebar, customize, upgrade, downloads or comment-*, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in location.hash, or the start view if none, on load and on hashchange. Keep other state in the page, and keys, tokens or private values out of the hash: it shows in history and copied links.
- Where this server lists a tool that describes page capabilities, call it before writing a page that needs downloads, a device, state that must last, or data that other viewers or devices must see: a capability may provide it. If none does, tell the user what cannot work, and do not fake it.

## Who can see it

A new artifact is visible to its owner only. This server cannot change who can see an artifact; the owner shares it from its page on claude.ai.

## Publishing

- Where this server lists a tool that publishes from files on disk and you can write files, that is the way to publish a page you write: write the page to a file in your working folder, then publish the file without stopping to ask, with title and icon. You write the page once, and the file is yours to look at and edit later.
- Where it lists none, where you cannot write files, or where that tool answers that the client cannot attach files: publish_version with title, icon and content, no slug.
- Either way the result carries slug, version and url.
- Small change to a page: edit_version with slug, base_version and edits. The server reads the page, replaces each old_text with its new_text, and publishes the result. Nothing is published if an edit does not apply.
- Small change to another text file of an artifact published from files, such as a stylesheet or a script: the same call with path. Every other file is kept. A JSON file must still parse after the edits, or nothing is published.
- Whole new page for an existing artifact: publish it as you would a new page, adding slug and base_version. Whichever way you publish it, the artifact's other files, if it has any, are kept and still served. A publish from files can also remove the ones the new page no longer uses.
- When the artifact's read value is users, org or public, every republish also passes shared_live with that word. It states who the artifact is already shared with and changes nothing.
- base_version is the version you last saw: from your last publish result, get_artifact or read_artifact. If someone published since, the call is refused with a conflict that names the live version. Do what the refusal's error sentence says. If it has none, read the artifact again, redo the change on the current page, and retry; never retry with the new version and your old content.
- Omit title and icon when republishing to keep them. Pass title only to rename.
- read_artifact reads a page the user owns, or one that belongs to someone in the user's organization and that the user can open. Where it refuses a page because of who has written to it, it names read_shared_artifact, and the user is asked first. A page the user does not own can be republished only with edit_version or publish_version, and only if it is in the user's organization, is not public, and the user can edit it.
- To read a page too large for one result, call read_artifact with offset and follow next_offset. A part is never the whole page: do not send it to publish_version.
- After a publish, say in one sentence what the page is, or what changed on a republish, and give the user the url. If your instructions or the publish result say the user's app already shows a card with the page's link, leave the url out unless the user asks for it.
- The published page is the delivery. If you wrote a file, keep it, but do not also send it to the user unless they ask for it.

## What is refused

- Artifacts of another organization, and ones the user does not own and cannot edit.
- Public artifacts the user does not own.
- By publish_version, and by edit_version without path: artifacts made from a type (a slide deck, a document, a design). Where this server offers a tool that publishes from files, it publishes the content files of one whose type keeps content in files, in patch mode, and edit_version with path replaces text in one of them; the type's own files cannot be changed.
- Artifacts that hold a live document.
- Content that is not HTML, or that embeds an archive or a PDF.

content.content:
**Relationship analysis.** The heaviest dependency roots are listed in the data line below; they are the project's bottlenecks. Command & Simulation Layer sits under almost everything because TD-FEASIBILITY made 'every mutation is an authority-checked request' the rule that keeps co-op additive. The Life-Support Graph is the data every visible system reads. The Item & Module Database is a quiet bottleneck: salvage, welding, save format, depletion and depth rings all need its definitions, so it should be designed early despite looking like content. Lighting is both a Foundation-adjacent technical risk and the carrier of three pillars. The Perception Filter is deliberately a query service with many readers and no simulation writers: it is the isolation that makes Sanity safe. The Emitter State & Light-Exposure Query exists for the mirror-image reason: light must stay a simulation input the Filter cannot touch. UI and Audio systems depend on gameplay systems, never the reverse, so they can be designed after the rules they display.

**Relationship analysis (data).** The four heaviest dependency roots are Command & Simulation Layer (16 dependents), Life-Support Graph (14 dependents), Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera (11 dependents), Item & Module Database (9 dependents).

> **Technical Director Review (TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY)**: CONCERNS, revisions applied 2026-10-25 — emitter state split from light rendering; Ship Section & Layout Data Model and Ship Body & Interior Physics added; Save/Load inverted into a state-block contract; Failure & Trail made a pure reader; Item DB sequenced after the Graph; Web Map & Transit owns the world model. GDD-level notes are carried in each system's rationale above.

content.content:
# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

**Relationship analysis.** The heaviest dependency roots are listed in the data line below; they are the project's bottlenecks. Command & Simulation Layer sits under almost everything because TD-FEASIBILITY made 'every mutation is an authority-checked request' the rule that keeps co-op additive. The Life-Support Graph is the data every visible system reads. The Item & Module Database is a quiet bottleneck: salvage, welding, save format, depletion and depth rings all need its definitions, so it should be designed early despite looking like content. Lighting is both a Foundation-adjacent technical risk and the carrier of three pillars. The Perception Filter is deliberately a query service with many readers and no simulation writers: it is the isolation that makes Sanity safe. The Emitter State & Light-Exposure Query exists for the mirror-image reason: light must stay a simulation input the Filter cannot touch. UI and Audio systems depend on gameplay systems, never the reverse, so they can be designed after the rules they display.

**Relationship analysis (data).** The four heaviest dependency roots are Command & Simulation Layer (16 dependents), Life-Support Graph (14 dependents), Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera (11 dependents), Item & Module Database (9 dependents).

> **Technical Director Review (TD-SYSTEM-BOUNDARY)**: CONCERNS, revisions applied 2026-10-25 — emitter state split from light rendering; Ship Section & Layout Data Model and Ship Body & Interior Physics added; Save/Load inverted into a state-block contract; Failure & Trail made a pure reader; Item DB sequenced after the Graph; Web Map & Transit owns the world model. # Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

print(f"edits {len(r['edits'])}: ok {ok}; new {len(r['new_entries'])}: added {added}; skipped {len(skipped)}; declined {len(r['declined'])}; failed batches {r.get('failed')}")
for x in skipped:
    print('SKIP', x['why'], x['name'], repr(x.get('old_text', '')[:80]))

"""Usage: python -I reg_hits.py <slug> [<slug> ...]
For each GDD design/gdd/<slug>.md, write tail/hits/<slug>.md listing every registry entry that the GDD
owns (source), is listed in referenced_by / pending comments, or whose exact name occurs in the text,
with the registry facts and up to 12 matching GDD lines (line numbers). Observations only, no verdicts."""
import re, sys, os
ROOT = 'D:/the-synaptic-sea-2d'
OUT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), 'hits')
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
reg = open(f'{ROOT}/design/registry/entities.yaml', encoding='utf-8').read().splitlines()
entries, cur, section = [], None, None
for i, l in enumerate(reg, 1):
    m = re.match(r'^(entities|items|formulas|constants):', l)
    if m: section = m.group(1); continue
    m = re.match(r'^  - name: (.+)$', l)
    if m:
        cur = {'name': m.group(1).strip().strip('"'), 'section': section, 'line': i, 'body': []}; entries.append(cur); continue
    if cur is not None and (l.startswith('    ') or l.startswith('#') or not l.strip()):
        if l.strip(): cur['body'].append(l.rstrip())
    elif cur is not None and l.strip():
        cur = None
for slug in sys.argv[1:]:
    path = f'design/gdd/{slug}.md'
    g = open(f'{ROOT}/{path}', encoding='utf-8').read().splitlines()
    out = [f'# Registry hits for {path} ({len(g)} lines; registry entries: {len(entries)})', '']
    n = 0
    for e in entries:
        body = '\n'.join(e['body'])
        owner = f'source: {path}' in body
        listed = path in body
        pat = re.compile(r'(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])' + re.escape(e['name']) + r'(?![A-Za-z0-9_])')

11:> **Amendments after the first design review (2026-10-27)**: four BLOCKING findings and the RECOMMENDED set were applied in place and every touched paragraph or row is marked *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: (1) the look-ahead / mouse-aim loop is opened by definition (C4, C11, D.7, D.14b); (2) every pose term settles per axis so a still scene's pose is constant (D.6, D.7, SETTLE_EPS); (3) the "identical at 60 and 144 fps" contract is replaced by a stated bound, with the lag measured after the update (C3, D.6); (4) the Y-sort tie-break is a class rank plus a stable entity ID, never `x` or creation order, with a rule for passable doors (PR-5, D.12). The RECOMMENDED set also changed: `τ_follow_eff = τ_follow × min(1, s)` with a zoom-step state transition; even logical fields; a world-anchored z-band fallback; a solver-written camera transform; BODY_TRANSFER rebase and an L = 0 wake; solver guards; draw-call caps per field; an analytic flash governor; picture-relative `world_to_hud`; PR-15 additions; and a rebuilt Dependencies table. No CD-GDD-ALIGN re-review was run.
162:**C5. Pan-speed ceiling and the cut rule (ux-designer, decided).** The camera's pan speed is ceilinged at **1.25 × `v_max`** (the avatar's fastest locomotion; amended from 1.25× walk — see the Section D amendment); if the follow term would exceed it for `T_PAN` = 0.10 s (6 frames at 60 fps), or the follow lag exceeds **`LAG_CUT` = 48 px**, the solver **cuts** (state reset to the target) rather than fast-panning; a **single-frame target jump ≥ 48 base px** (one tile) cuts immediately. These predicates are **backstops**, not tuning for ordinary movement: at MVP no legal locomotion reaches them (a `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` = 4 catch-up delivers at most 4 ticks × 3 px = 12 px, below `JUMP_CUT` and below the 225 px/s ceiling), so they fire only for named sources — a weld `frame_delta_px` that was not rebased, a Body shove or knock that displaces the avatar without a walk, hitch recovery (`dt` beyond `DT_MAX` followed by a burst), a restore, or a zoom-step rescale that were ever skipped — and the fixtures that exercise them are explicitly synthetic. The camera **teleports (full solver state reset to the target)** on every `LOADING → RUNNING` and every pod or transit body transfer (gameplay-programmer, ux-designer); a weld or detach `BODY_TRANSFER` that carries a `frame_delta_px` is instead a **rebase**: the solver shifts `f` and its history by `frame_delta_px` into the new body frame and **keeps the lag and `L`**, so the avatar's screen position does not move (zeroing the lag shifted the avatar by up to 32 px), and only a transfer whose hull jump cannot be guaranteed zero (BDY-27, Edge Cases) is hidden by a hard cut, never a pan. After a `LOADING → RUNNING` or a wake the solver starts with **`L = 0` and eases it in** at the slew rate, so the first frame is `pose_q = quantise(target)` whatever the aim was at the instant of the cut and re-wake framing is reproducible; a cut the solver triggers itself (`P_pan`, `P_lag`, `P_jump`) resets `f` and keeps `L`, because the lean is player-caused *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. **Camera state is never persisted**; after a restore the solver starts from the target. Because the solver interpolates from previous/current, every owner of a moving read view must set `previous := current` in `post_restore` so the first frame after a load does not interpolate from a stale pose — routed to the kernel (CR-10 / CR-8 `post_restore`) and Save/Load.
164:**C6. Zoom: integer ladder in both directions, persistent, cut not tween.** `Camera2D.zoom` stays `(1,1)`; "zoom" is a change of the world's integer scale: press `zoom_in` / `zoom_out` (edge-triggered; one step per press; persistent — never held — and reset to default on re-wake) to step `k` through the integer ladder `[1, k_base + 2]` (user decision 2026-10-26, supersedes the game-designer's single held step out); it is available in every state including breach (it is a player input, C1). At 1080p the ladder is 1×, 2×, **3× default**, 4×, 5× (sprites at 33 / 67 / 100 / 133 / 167 %); 8.1's "one integer step out" is the first `zoom_out` press (amendment routed to art-director). C-R's "no zoom-out below a 2× world" is **superseded**: on a 2× world (720p, Steam Deck, manual 2×) the ladder reaches 1× (decided 2026-10-26, creative director concurs, user ratification pending — Open Question 4; on-device acuity check routed to the accessibility-specialist). The logical size at a ladder step `k_z` is `picture / k_z`, **uncapped** (PR-2's cap applies to default zoom only; at 1440p one step out is 1280×720 logical, and letterboxing it would defeat the step); at 1080p one step out is 960×540 = 20 × 11.25 tiles, so the 8 × 6 machine room of 8.2 fits, and 1× is 1920×1080 base = 40 × 22.5 tiles. The solver's length parameters scale with the field (`s = field_h / 360`, D.6–D.10) so the camera feels the same at every step. The change is a **cut**: one frame at the old k, the next at the new, no intermediate scale (none is integer), no zoom pulse. The HUD does not change (PR-12). Zoom-in **is** offered as integer steps up to `k_base + 2` (user decision 2026-10-26 — see the zoom-ladder note; the tight default frame remains the default, not the only frame). Every step is implemented by changing the world viewport's **logical size** (pass A: `size`; pass B: `size_2d_override`), never `Camera2D.zoom` — which shares the unresolved wiring question of PR-7 (two integer scales in one window under one root stretch) and is folded into spike step 11. **"Across the room" readability** (Pillar 2's frosting elbow seen to worsen from across the room) is satisfied by trail propagation into frame, look-ahead, wide-and-shallow kits (8.2) and the player's zoom steps — **never by a wider default frame** (game-designer). *Playtest metric:* the share of boarding time spent away from default zoom, in either direction; **> 50 % → revisit the default frame** (routed to game-designer and the playtest plan). *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check: held-step wording replaced by the edge-triggered ladder throughout.)* **Input pacing.** A wheel burst can deliver dozens of notches in one frame, so the pipeline root accepts **at most one step per frame and at least `ZOOM_STEP_MIN_INTERVAL` = 0.15 s between accepted steps**, and discards the surplus (never queued; `diag.zoom_step_rate_limited` counts them); a button press is subject to the same interval. **`k_base` rule.** The ladder is built on `k_base` — the manual `k` when Settings sets one below Auto, else `k_auto` — and `k_base` is the default step, the `k` of the pinned HUD rect's picture (and **not** of `H_default`, which stays `max(k_auto, 3)`: a manual smaller world scale never shrinks the HUD); with a manual `k` the aspect is `keep` (PR-2), so a manual-2× player at 1080p has the ladder 1×–4× and the default frame of a 2× player, not a permanently wider one. **MVP death stub.** At MVP the failure state is the death stub — restart from the last autosave (user decision) — an in-session `LOADING → RUNNING` restore in place: the camera `CUT`s at the **pre-load `k_z`** (zoom is pipeline state and is not reset; only the VS-A re-wake resets it, C10), with `L` starting at 0 and easing in *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*.
175:- *Crew loss and re-wake.* 2.10's sources going out one by one is Lighting reading state; the camera **holds exactly where it was until the hard cut** (no drift, no pull-in); on `LOADING` the pipeline shows layer 1 black; on `RUNNING` it cuts to the new avatar under the cryo-bay lamp with **framing identical to the first wake — snap, not ease** (game-designer; 2.2: "I know this room" before "something has changed"); `L` starts at 0 and eases in (C5), so the framing is reproducible whatever the aim was. **MVP:** the failure state is the death stub, a restart from the last autosave — an in-session restore in place (`LOADING → RUNNING`, a hard `CUT` at the pre-load `k_z`, C6), not the VS-A re-wake; it has no lights-out beat and does not reset zoom *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*.
274:**Camera states** (the `CameraSolver`'s state machine; every transition is a player input, a kernel state change or a solver rule — never world state, C1). **The camera's state is three independent fields, not one enum** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: **follow** ∈ {`FOLLOWING`, `CLAMPED`} (`CLAMPED` if either axis is clamped, driven only by the limits rect and the unclamped pose), **zoom** ∈ {default, `ZOOMED`} (`k_z ≠ k_base`, driven only by presses and `RESCALING`), and **hold** ∈ {live, `HELD`, `CUT`} (driven only by kernel and pipeline state and the cut rules). The rows below name the common combinations; every combination is legal and the transitions are independent: a zoom step changes only the zoom field (and is a `RESCALING` frame that re-derives the field, rescales the solver state per D.6 and re-evaluates the clamp, so a step can move `FOLLOWING` to `CLAMPED` and back); a `CUT` clears the smoothing history and the jolt but never the zoom field (except the VS-A re-wake) and never the follow field's rect; `HELD` freezes the pose without clearing zoom or clamp, and `PAUSED_FROZEN → PAUSED` resumes to live with no `CUT`; `LOADING` holds, and `RUNNING` cuts. Missing transitions made explicit: `ZOOMED` + `CLAMPED` is legal; a zoom press while `HELD` is discarded (Edge Cases); a rebase (`BODY_TRANSFER` with `frame_delta_px`) is a live-to-live transition that shifts state and clears nothing.
280:| `ZOOMED` (formerly `ZOOMED_OUT`) | as `FOLLOWING`/`CLAMPED` with the world at the ladder step `k_z ∈ [1, k_base + 2]`, `k_z ≠ k_base`, logical size `picture / k_z`; every step is a one-frame **cut** (`RESCALING`); the solver's length parameters are scaled by `s = field_h / 360` (`τ_follow` by `min(1, s)`; D.6–D.10) and the solver state is rescaled on the step's `RESCALING` frame (lag by the `τ_eff` ratio, `L` by `s_new/s_old`, D.6) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | yes | `zoom_out` pressed while `k_z > 1`, or `zoom_in` pressed while `k_z < k_base + 2` (edge-triggered; one step per press; persistent, never held; a press beyond either end is ignored and `diag.zoom_step_refused` increments) | `FOLLOWING`/`CLAMPED` when a press returns `k_z` to `k_base`; **re-wake resets `k_z` to `k_base`** (through that `CUT`); otherwise the step survives `CUT` (body transfer, in-session load, transit), `HELD` and `PAUSED_FROZEN`; a `RESCALING` that changes `k_base` rebuilds the ladder and clamps `k_z` to its ends *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check)* |
281:| `CUT` | teleport: solver `f` reset to the target; `L` reset to 0 and eased in on a wake or load (kept on a solver-initiated cut); jolt cleared; smoothing history cleared *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review: was "look-ahead at full value")* | no — the first frame is final | `TRANSIT_HOLD` ending; every `LOADING → RUNNING`; re-wake (framing identical to first wake); a pod or transit body transfer, or a weld/detach whose hull jump is not guaranteed zero; the solver's own cut rule — pan ceiling exceeded ≈ 6 frames, lag > 48 px, or target jump ≥ 48 px in one frame (C5, backstops). A weld/detach `BODY_TRANSFER` with `frame_delta_px` is a **rebase**, not a `CUT` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | `FOLLOWING` (or `CLAMPED` if the new body has limits) |
512:**Example:** Re-wake: the target moves ≈ 2 000 px in one frame → `P_jump` → cut. A synthetic 40 px burst (no legal walk produces one; a weld delta or a Body shove could): `P_jump` false; initial `v_follow = 40 / 0.18 = 222 px/s`, **below** the 225 px/s ceiling, so `P_pan` never arms → no cut; D.8 pins the avatar inside the box while D.6 eases. A 47 px burst (just under `JUMP_CUT`): initial `v_follow = 261 px/s > 225`, back below the ceiling at `t = 0.18 × ln(261/225) = 0.027 s < T_PAN` → no cut. Running at 180 px/s: lag 32.4 px, `v_follow = 180 < 225` → no predicate fires. *(Re-run 2026-10-26 — consistency check.)*

The design review of all 26 MVP GDDs is finished: 2 GDDs passed, 23 still need revision after one fix-and-re-review pass, and Boarding & Salvage needs major revision. Most of what's still open is waiting on rulings from you, not more review.

**Your decisions are on this page:** https://claude.ai/artifact/UNo92EM7YkgjjWc7YDi63c. There are 98 decisions across the GDDs, but many repeat the same question, so the page groups them into 13 shared rulings, ordered by how much each unblocks. It also lists every GDD's remaining blockers, decisions and reviewer disagreements.

**Verdicts**
- **Approved (2):** Ship Section & Layout Data Model, and Sanity & Hallucination Rules. Sanity still has 6 open decisions, but none of them block approval.
- **Needs Revision (23):** 58 blockers remain across them.
- **Major Revision (1): Boarding & Salvage.** Two pillar-level failures:
  - The anchor moment, carrying salvage home while Attention rises, never happens. The reference sortie only reaches 57–65% of the Attention threshold, so no tell fires.
  - No GDD guarantees that a sortie can't get stuck at a dark dock. Interaction refused the lit exemption for the hop, and Web Map declined the stricter content check.

  Both need rulings that span several GDDs (shared rulings 2 and 3 on the page).

**The most urgent rulings:**
1. **MVP scope:** one weld only, or weld + cut + install. This blocks the start of the spike.
2. **Getting home from a dark dock:** which mechanism guarantees the hop.
3. **The carry tell:** how the carry under rising Attention actually gets delivered.
4. **`top_up` verb:** whether it's in MVP. This decides whether the lamp cell and the "go dark" lever exist.
5. **`tool_suppressant`:** whether it stays in the start kit, given it does nothing at MVP.
6. **Autosave and a dying crew:** whether vitals at CRITICAL hold back the autosave.
7. **Reference machine:** naming one, so the performance criteria can be judged.

The page has the other six, covering the suit alarm, accessibility for deaf or muted players, the sanity rim fringe, hearing range, and the kernel's ratification batch.

**Weaker coverage on some reviews:** 29 of the 160 specialist agents returned nothing. Horror Entities was reviewed by only the AI programmer, Derelict Authoring lost three specialists, and seven GDDs had no QA lead. The creative director knew which were missing when giving verdicts. The review logs had wrongly listed the failed specialists as consulted, and I've corrected all 19 affected logs.

**Registry**
- 266 change requests from the fixers were applied: 139 new entries and about 190 changed. It now has 972 entries and passes the project's validator.
- 7 requests are parked. Two wait on your rulings (`SUPPRESSANT_START_CHARGES`, `BEAM_SPILL_PM`); the rest needed no change. 6 more were declined as not matching their GDD's text.
- I quoted 15 values so the file loads with a standard YAML parser. It didn't load before this session.
- A consistency check of the changed entries fixed 58 places where other GDDs no longer matched the owning GDD. The two approved GDDs weren't touched. Boarding had 7 cited values realigned; no design fix.

Because of those later edits, every review record is now out of date, so the next `/design-review` will treat all 26 GDDs as changed. That's expected.

**Diffstat:** 28 files changed, 9,796 insertions and 5,594 deletions:
- the 26 GDDs, `systems-index.md` and `entities.yaml`;
- plus the new, untracked `design/gdd/reviews/` (26 review logs).

`.claude/workflows/` stays out of the commit. The decision log and the consistency-failures log are updated; both are local and gitignored.

Say "commit and push" when you want this committed. After that, the next step is your rulings on the page. `/review-all-gdds` and `/gate-check` come after those.

[D1] command-simulation-layer: Open Question 18: ratify or reject every adopted/proposed item in one batched pass (R-1..R-20: ticks_for_seconds rounding, host_order, never-stale invariant, paused service cycle as a retained seam, coalescing and frozen semantics, seq gaps, SYSTEM results to log only, tolerates_stale warning, TICK_RATE header mismatch, the new Faulted terminal and fault-result semantics, catch-up P5 merge, control-plane timing, mandatory registration fields, payload whitelist, TickDriver design, H64/mix64/fnv64 choices, knob reclassification, frame budgets, MAX_BLOCKS and log capacity). Existing markers were left in place for the user to clear.

[D2] command-simulation-layer: Open Question 19: lag forgiveness policy. (A) keep LAG_FORGIVE_TICKS = 30 (repays up to 30 ticks at up to 4x over up to 10 frames; current text), (B, recommended) LAG_FORGIVE_TICKS = 0, never fast-forward at all, which matches the creative-director note literally, or (C) drop only the excess above the threshold. The spec is written parametric and defaults to (A) pending the answer.

[D3] command-simulation-layer: Open Question 21 (inside R-12): confirm merging PRESENTATION/PROJECTOR/DIAGNOSTIC notification batches into one per catch-up frame (INPUT_SURFACE, REPLICATION and control-plane callers keep per-tick batches). This was a designer decision taken in this review.

[D4] command-simulation-layer: Open Question 22: name the minimum-spec reference machine for the performance ACs and FRAME_SIM_BUDGET_MS.

[D5] pixel-perfect-render-pipeline-camera: Open Question 21 (contingent): if the spike shows a zoom-out ladder step cannot meet the per-field draw cap (D.16) and the P99 frame-time ceiling on the reference hardware, either the lowest failing step(s) are withheld or the content/costs change. Withholding narrows the user's zoom-in/zoom-out ladder decision, so only the user can choose it. Nothing is decided now; no blocker needs a decision today.

[D6] player-controller-input: OQ 19: cost of retreating with the beam on the pursuer. Options A accept twin-stick retreat (tension claim already struck), B weight camera look-ahead towards movement while running (presentation only; game-designer lean), C playtest an exposure/noise cost for aiming backwards.

[D7] player-controller-input: OQ 20: solo DOWNED recovery. Keep ~30 s wait, or solo-only DOWN_TO_DEATH_TICKS of 120-180, or a 'give up and reload' action while downed (1800 kept for the VS-B revive window). Does not change the 'MVP death = restart from last autosave' decision.

[D8] player-controller-input: OQ 21: default for the pad aim_release_mode: FOLLOW_MOVE_WHEN_RELEASED (design lean), HOLD (previously decided amendment 9, current placeholder) or FOLLOW_ALWAYS.

[D9] player-controller-input: OQ 26: whether to add an opt-in, off-by-default aim indicator accessibility setting, which would reopen HUD HS-52 / HS-DT-2 (no cursor/reticle/aim line).

[D10] player-controller-input: Interpretive note for the user: the 2026-10-26 decision 'mouse aim is the direction from the chest point to the cursor' is honoured as a fixed reference chest (AIM_ORIGIN) with the beam still drawn from the true chest point; confirm this reading is acceptable.

[D11] life-support-graph: USER DECISION (confirm; non-blocking, default applied) - Open Question 30, inert make-up source: the Graph now has the scrubber supply inert make-up (demand-driven, accounted in produced_mgu) so a patched room always recovers while the scrubber runs. Alternative: a finite inert reserve in each O2_TANK, so a breach permanently costs gas until a tank is salvaged. This changes how scarce air feels (Pillar 5, Depth Rings & Scarcity) and would need an Item DB / Derelict Authoring field. The creative-director's literal 'standard air' option was not adopted because it cannot sustain respiration.

Creative director recommends (b); the document defaults to (a) until decided.

[D20] emitter-state-and-light-exposure-query: OQ 1: beacon gates_actions false (a strobing prompt would lie, P1). Creative-director supports keeping it. Put to the user before sprint planning, then clear the provisional flag.

[D22] emitter-state-and-light-exposure-query: OQ 3: depth in the web never changes beam reach (art bible fixed-anchor principle). Keep?

It touches the chest-lamp decision, so the shipped default stays 0 until the user confirms. Validate with the dark-at-feet playtest metric; 24 px does not cover an object one tile to the side.

I need to build out a ruling sheet: for each decision, go with the recommended option where one exists, otherwise pick a sensible default and label it "Claude's pick" so the user can see it clearly, and leave genuinely fact-dependent items (like the reference machine specs) open for the user to answer.

On the dark dock conflict, Boarding wants M1 (a console-only lit exemption) while Web Map wants B (treating status glow as a lit fixture, no new exemption). I lean toward Web Map's B since it preserves the lit-only invariant and avoids creating a fourth exception Interaction already rejected, though it does mean promoting top_up into the MVP per Boarding's cell policy. For the carry tell decision, I'm weighing three options and leaning toward B, which adds a new carry intake mechanic that literally delivers on the "carry it home under rising Attention" fantasy better than the alternatives.
